# []{#anchor}Results

## []{#anchor-1}**Climate and Well Network Characterization**

### []{#anchor-2}**Climate Record**

The RAF Valley climate station provides a continuous monthly record from December 1930 to February 2026 (Figure 4a+b) (Section 3.1.2). Over the well-record period (April 2005 to February 2026), mean annual precipitation was 891 mm and mean annual Thornthwaite PET was 653 mm, giving a mean P/PET ratio of 1.37 (Table 1). The wettest year on record within this period was 2008 (1,040 mm), followed by 2012 (1,022 mm); the driest complete year was 2010 (736 mm). Two years recorded a P/PET ratio below 1.2 --- indicating near-balance between precipitation and evaporative demand --- namely 2011 and 2022, with 2022 recording the lowest ratio of the monitoring period at 1.11; 2010 (1.20) and 2007 (1.22) sat close to that line. There is no meaningful difference in mean annual precipitation between the pre-felling (2006--2017: 887 mm) and post-felling (2018--2025: 896 mm) periods.

PET shows strong seasonality but negligible inter-annual trend across the record, with the 12-month rolling mean remaining stable at approximately 50--55 mm/month throughout (Figure 4b).

The levelled cumulative water balance series (Figure 4c), expressed relative to the study-period mean of 19.51 mm/month, oscillates with a clear seasonal signal --- rising sharply each winter as precipitation exceeds PET and falling each summer --- while tracking the multi-year rhythm of wetter and drier phases. No sustained multi-year drift away from the baseline is evident. The water table clearly follows this movement (Figure 4d). Linear regression of the cumulative balance against the unsmoothed network mean water level at zero lag yielded R² = 0.527. This close correspondence between cumulative climate forcing and water table behaviour provided the empirical motivation for the state-space modelling framework described in Section 3.4.

Mean monthly rainfall peaks in October--December (around 101--109 mm/month) and falls to its minimum in April (around 46 mm/month; Figure 4a), whilst Thornthwaite (1957) PET peaks in July (around 107 mm/month) and is negligible from November to February (Figure 4b). Over the monitoring period, mean annual winter rainfall (October--March) was 518 mm and mean annual summer rainfall (April--September) was 373 mm, together summing to the 891 mm annual mean.

The RAF Valley record also shows a statistically significant warming trend in mean summer maximum temperature over the full 95-year record (slope +0.014°C yr⁻¹, R² = 0.142, p \< 0.001; Figure 5). The post-2013 period has run 0.94°C above the pre-2013 baseline mean of 17.89°C, with six of the thirteen summers between 2013 and 2025 exceeding this baseline by more than 1°C (2013, 2018, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2025). The most extreme anomalies occurred in 2022 (+1.77°C) and 2023 (+1.64°C). The year 2022 combined a +1.77°C temperature anomaly with only 747 mm annual rainfall --- the most severe dual-stress year in the monitoring period. Annual rainfall shows no significant trend over the full record (p = 0.498).

### []{#anchor-3}**4.1.2 Well Network**

The 66-well reference network (Section 3.1.1) spans a median record length of 191 months (15.9 years), with individual cleaned series ranging from 139 to 250 months (Figure 6, upper left); all wells satisfy the 100-month minimum-observation threshold for admission to the reference network. The network mean water level across all wells and months was 0.77 m below ground --- water levels throughout are reported as depth below the ground surface (negative below ground, positive when ponded above ground) --- with individual well means ranging from 0.26 m to 2.07 m below, reflecting the considerable topographic and hydrogeological diversity of the site (Figure 6, upper right). The median seasonal amplitude --- defined as the difference between mean August and mean February water levels --- was 0.69 m, with the water table deepest in late summer and shallowest in late winter, consistent with the expected seasonal recharge cycle for a maritime dune system (Figure 6, lower right). The network mean time series (Figure 6, lower left) shows a clear seasonal cycle throughout the record, with the inter-well standard deviation envelope widening visibly after the December 2017 clearfell intervention, reflecting the divergence of the impact zone wells from the broader network that is explored in detail in Section 4.6.

Mapped against the eco-hydrological thresholds of Curreli et al. (2013), the network-wide seasonal extremes fall largely outside the viable range. The mean annual summer minimum across the reference network was −1.18 m below ground, ranging from −0.71 m to −2.32 m across individual wells. No well maintains a mean summer minimum shallower than the wet slack viability threshold of −0.61 m; 28 wells fall within the dry slack zone (−0.61 to −0.98 m); and 38 wells record mean summer minima deeper than the dry slack threshold of −0.98 m, of which 20 lie below the SD16 recovery limit of −1.20 m --- placing them beyond the reach of a single scraping event under average conditions. For winter maxima, 25 wells exceed the SD15b wet slack flooding threshold of −0.10 m in an average year and 38 exceed the SD16 dry slack threshold of −0.25 m, though only 11 record mean winter maxima above ground. These network-level baselines provide the reference against which cluster-specific dynamics, intervention effects, and climate trajectory are assessed in subsequent sections.

## []{#anchor-4}Network Clustering and Spatial Architecture

The clustering analysis (Section 3.2) identified k = 5 as the preferred cluster solution (silhouette coefficient = 0.40; bootstrap stability analysis confirming four of five clusters with median per-well co-assignment ≥ 0.93). The five clusters are spatially coherent and hydrogeologically interpretable (Table 3; Figures 7--9); their mechanistic characterization including LCSC values is presented in Section 4.2.2.

The dendrogram confirms a primary binary division separating eastern wells (C1, C2) from western and forest wells (C3, C4, C5) at a Ward linkage distance of approximately 1.0. The forest clusters (C4 Main Forest, C5 Coastal Forest) separate from adjacent C3 wells despite geographical proximity. The separation also reflects the position of the C4 wells in the northern part of the study area, closest to the rock ridge, at the highest topographic positions in the dune system. C5 (Coastal Forest) occupies the coastal edge of the plantation where canopy and coastal influences combine.

### []{#anchor-5}  Cluster Hydrographs and Seasonal Amplitudes

The five cluster average hydrographs (Figure 9b) reveal a clear stratification of groundwater behaviour that reflects the hydrogeological architecture identified by the clustering analysis. C1 (Lake Edge) shows the shallowest mean depth (−0.38 m). The one exception within C1 is CEH11, assigned to the cluster on hydrograph similarity but geographically isolated on the south-eastern coast, so its mechanistic coefficients are not interpreted alongside the lake-edge wells (Section 3.2.3). C2 (Dune) tracks C1 closely but sits systematically deeper (mean −0.60 m). The fundamental geological contrast between the Eastern and Western Blocks is visible as a persistent vertical offset between C1/C2 and C3 (Western Residual), with C3 running approximately 0.3 m deeper on average (mean −0.89 m) despite occupying a broadly similar topographic position. C4 (Main Forest) is the most distinctive cluster, sitting 0.6 m deeper than adjacent C3 wells throughout the record (mean −1.47 m). The C4 cluster mean hydrograph should be interpreted cautiously prior to 2010, when only three of the nine cluster wells were operational (CEH2, CEH13 and NW10); these wells are disproportionately located at higher elevations on the ridge margin so the apparent high mean heads in 2006--2008 reflect an unrepresentative spatial sample rather than a genuine network-wide signal. Full nine-well coverage was not achieved until mid-2010. C5 (Coastal Forest) sits at comparable depth to C4 (mean −1.25 m) but with a damped seasonal signal. Across all five clusters the average hydrographs (Figure 9b) follow the levelled cumulative water balance (Figure 9a) throughout the record. Per-well seasonal amplitudes and their temporal evolution are analysed below.

The network mean water table elevation was 7.45 m AOD across the 66-well reference network (elevations computed as water level above each well's NRW 2 m LiDAR-derived ground surface; Section 3.1.1), ranging from 3.02 m AOD (CEH11, C1 Lake Edge) to 13.32 m AOD at the ridge flank (CEH14, C4 Main Forest). CEH11\'s assignment to C1 is discussed in Section 3.2.3: its low elevation and coastal position place it near the Menai Strait tidal boundary rather than Llyn Rhos-Ddu, and it represents the low-elevation extreme of the reference network rather than a typical lake-edge well. Excluding CEH11, the C1 cluster-mean elevation rises from 8.46 m AOD to 9.37 m AOD, and the network minimum shifts to CEH21 (C3, 3.10 m AOD). The Main Forest cluster (C4) occupies the highest mean water table elevation in the network at 9.24 m AOD, compared with 8.46 m AOD in the Lake Edge cluster (C1), 7.50 m AOD in the Dune cluster (C2), and 7.00 m AOD in the Western Residual (C3). The Coastal Forest cluster (C5) sits at 4.39 m AOD, the lowest cluster-mean elevation in the network.

Climate-normalized values exclude empirically-identified drought summers (2005, 2018, 2022) where Jun--Sep rainfall fell ≥1σ below the 1931--2017 baseline. (Source: 02_09_cluster_amplitude_summary.csv)

**

Three patterns emerge. First, the open dune clusters (C2, C3) show stable raw amplitude but modest climate-normalized damping (≈8--9%), consistent with the post-2018 drought summers temporarily inflating apparent variability while the underlying seasonal range has slightly contracted. Second, **C5 Coastal Forest shows a pronounced amplitude collapse** of 18% (raw) to 21% (climate-normalized), the largest reduction in the network: recharge peaks no longer reach their pre-2018 heights even after correcting for drought summers (Section 5.7.2). Third, **C1 Lake Edge shows the opposite pattern**: amplitude has *increased* by 15--19%, driven primarily by deeper summer minima rather than higher winter peaks (median post-2018 summer minimum −1.04 m vs −1.42 m at C3; Table 2). The C3 cluster shows the highest within-cluster spread (post-2018 ratio max:min ≈ 2.0), approaching the amplitude-heterogeneity flagging threshold (Section 3.2.4).

The amplitude analysis shows that the cluster-mean coefficients reported in Section 4.2.2 represent stable averages across wells whose individual amplitude responses differ within most clusters by less than a factor of two, but with sufficient within-cluster variation in C3 and C4 to motivate the per-well coefficient mapping presented in Section 4.9.

### []{#anchor-6}Cluster Mechanistic Characterization

The five clusters are characterized mechanistically in Table 3 using a state-space model fitted to the average hydrograph for each cluster (Section 3.4.1); Table 4 gives the range of the per-well fits that each centroid summarises, so the spread behind every coefficient below is visible alongside it. β₁ is the recharge sensitivity --- the water table rise (mm) per mm of rainfall; β₂ is the atmospheric draw --- the water table decline (mm) per mm of PET; and −β₃ is the proportional drainage decay rate --- the fraction of antecedent displacement above the drainage datum (Section 3.4) dissipated by lateral drainage each month. All five cluster-centroid coefficient sets reported in Table 3 are statistically significant (p \< 0.01); within-cluster, individual per-well coefficients vary in significance, most notably the near-zero C4 drainage coefficient and the small C1 atmospheric-draw term, as discussed below and in Section 4.9.

The recharge sensitivity coefficient β₁ is highest in the Lake Edge cluster (C1: 4.58), indicating that each millimetre of rainfall drives a proportionally larger water table rise in the shallow-till aquifer than in the Dune cluster (C2: 3.97) or Western Residual (C3: 3.57). The two forested clusters return near-identical and substantially lower recharge sensitivities (C4: 2.48, C5: 2.43). The atmospheric draw coefficient β₂ is highest at C4 (2.56), followed by C3 (1.81) and C2 (1.74), with C5 (1.27) and C1 (0.92) lowest. The C4 value of β₂ slightly exceeds its β₁ (2.56 against 2.48), meaning that the Main Forest cluster loses as much water table per mm of PET as it gains per mm of rainfall. Because β coefficients fold together vegetation effects, specific yield and soil moisture dynamics, they cannot be decomposed into crop coefficients without independent Sy estimates; this decomposition is developed in Section 5.6.1. C5 (Coastal Forest) has low β₂ despite also carrying Corsican pine canopy (Section 5.6.1). C1\'s β₂ (0.92) is the lowest in the network; the depth-dependent PET diagnostic (Section 3.7.1) returns the strongest residual depth-coupling at C1 (κ = 2.25 m⁻¹). The drainage decay coefficient −β₃ is highest at C1 (0.089), similar at C2 (0.064) and C3 (0.057), lower at C5 (0.045), and lowest at C4 (0.018). The C4 value is the smallest in the network, but it is well resolved at the cluster scale: the drainage and climate predictors are nearly uncorrelated at C4 (variance inflation factor ≈ 1.1) and the cluster carries the network\'s largest displacement variation, so the centroid coefficient is significant (p = 0.002; Section 5.2.3). Two ridge-flank wells, CEH13 and CEH14, return drainage coefficients indistinguishable from zero over their full records; excluding them from the cluster fit raises the coefficient to 0.029 month⁻¹, reported as a sensitivity in Section 5.2.3 rather than adopted as the cluster value. The LCSC (= 100/β₁) expresses these contrasts as a directly interpretable management metric: 22--25 mm of rainfall is required to raise Lake Edge and Dune water tables by 10 cm, compared with 28 mm in the Western Residual and 40--41 mm beneath the plantation.

The C1 cluster-mean coefficients in Table 3 include CEH11, which is geographically separated from the other six C1 members (Section 3.2.3). CEH11 sits at 3.6 m AOD on the south-eastern coast, approximately 1.6 km from the nearest lake-edge well, with a damped hydrograph (Section 5.1.1). Its β₂ value of 0.77 is consistent with the C1 cluster mean (0.96). CEH11\'s inclusion extends the C1 elevation range from 8.6--10.9 m down to 3.6 m; if excluded, the six remaining wells (five excluding CEH6, whose small negative β₂ (−0.39, non-significant at p = 0.28) is the only such coefficient in the network, and the reason the C1 β₂ range in Table 4 is the one range in the network that crosses zero; it is examined in Section 5.2.3) occupy a tight 9.1--10.9 m elevation band. The cluster-mean coefficients are not materially affected by CEH11\'s inclusion --- its β₁ (4.46) and β₃ (0.092) are close to the C1 mean --- but per-well spatial analyses within C1 should be interpreted with awareness that CEH11 responds to a different boundary condition.

An extended form of the state-space model incorporating a depth-dependent evapotranspiration coefficient (Section 3.7.1) was evaluated at cluster level; as the results of this analysis bear primarily on the mechanistic interpretation of the Forest cluster β₂ coefficient, they are discussed in Section 5.6.1 rather than reported here. The within-cluster coefficient variation is substantial, particularly in the forest zone where per-well β₂ ranges from 0.797 to 3.828 across the 14 C4 and C5 wells. Whether this variation tracks topographic position (a proxy for the uncored substrate) or canopy differences is examined through per-well spatial regression in Section 4.9.4.

The elevated C4 atmospheric-draw coefficient (β₂ = 2.56, the largest in the network) is accompanied by the network\'s lowest drainage coefficient (β₃ = 0.018 month⁻¹), so that at the cluster centroid the C4 loss budget is atmospheric-draw-dominated (ET ≈ 76%, drainage ≈ 24%). The identifiability of this low β₃ is examined in Section 5.2.3; the partition remains dependent on the drainage datum and substrate assumption, and is flagged as modelled and unconfirmed wherever it enters downstream analysis.

The identifiability of the C4 drainage coefficient was tested directly (Script 30). The variance inflation factor on the displacement term at the C4 centroid is 1.10 and the correlation between PET and displacement −0.04, against 1.82 and −0.61 at C1, 1.40 and −0.43 at C2, 1.27 and −0.32 at C3, and 1.08 and −0.17 at C5; C4 carries the network\'s largest displacement variation (standard deviation 0.48 m), and the centroid coefficient is significant (p = 0.002). Per well, the median variance inflation factor at C4 is 1.20 on the 100-month window, the lowest in the network; the per-well correlation between β₂ and β₃ is −0.77 across all nine wells, −0.32 with CEH14 removed and −0.27 with CEH13 and CEH14 both removed. The three wells whose β₃ is significant on the window (NW10, CEH20, CEH30) span 0.026--0.041 month⁻¹. At the fitted centroid coefficient of 0.018 month⁻¹ the steady-state water balance closes to a residual of 0.02% of the C4 loss budget (Section 4.2.3), and swept across β₃ that residual is minimised at 0.019 month⁻¹. Excluding the two ridge-flank wells raises the centroid from 0.018 to 0.029 month⁻¹ and shortens the recession time 1/β₃ from 54 to 34 months. The reading of these diagnostics is in Section 5.2.3.

Water balance decomposition applied to all five clusters (Section 3.7.2) reveals markedly different recharge sensitivities across clusters receiving nearly identical climate forcing. The head-space decomposition is presented in Table 5 and Figure 11; an indicative volumetric conversion is presented in Table 7 and Figure 11b. The derivation and defence of the specific yield values is addressed in Section 4.2.4.

Recharge into the water table (β₁·Pl) declines systematically from the Lake Edge cluster (C1: 0.340 m/month) through the Dune (C2: 0.295 m/month) and Western Residual (C3: 0.265 m/month) to the forested clusters (C5: 0.180 m/month; C4: 0.184 m/month). Total losses (atmospheric draw plus drainage) track recharge closely in every cluster. Residuals are less than 1.8% of total losses in all clusters. The drainage partition varies markedly across clusters: drainage accounts for 85% of total losses at C1 but only 24% at C4, where atmospheric draw dominates. C2 and C3 show drainage-dominated partitions (68%/32% and 63%/37% respectively), while C5 is intermediate (62%/38%).

Coefficients are cluster-centroid fits from the displacement-formulation SSM (Table 3). The head-space decomposition of Table 5 is one way to split the losses into evapotranspiration and drainage, and it inherits whatever uncertainty attaches to β₂ and β₃ separately. A second, model-independent estimate comes from the observed seasonal recession of the cluster means themselves (Section 3.7.2): the mean month-on-month decline over winter months in which the water table fell (November--February, when potential evapotranspiration is small) as a share of the same quantity in summer (June--September) estimates the drainage fraction of summer losses. Both terms are head declines, so specific yield cancels in the ratio and the estimate is independent of the WTF specific yields of Section 4.2.4. The two estimators are compared in Table 6. They agree to 1.3 percentage points at C3 (0.64 against 0.63) and to 11 points at C5 (0.74 against 0.62), and diverge by 21 to 25 points at C1, C2 and C4. C4 Main Forest reverses the ordering: the head-space ratio makes the forest interior much the most evapotranspiration-dominated cluster in the network (drainage fraction 0.24) while the recession ratio places it near the middle (0.49). Two acknowledged biases in the recession estimator --- winter potential evapotranspiration is small but not zero, and head-dependent drainage is faster in winter when heads are high --- both act to inflate its drainage fraction, so it is read as leaning high rather than as a point estimate. The spread between the two, not either alone, is the partition uncertainty carried into Table 7 and drawn as the hatched band of Figure 11b.

### []{#anchor-8}**Specific Yield Estimation**

WTF event-based median Sy estimates for all five clusters, derived from 35--62 qualifying monthly rising-limb events per cluster, are presented in Table 8, and the full event-level distribution behind each cluster median in Figure 12. A month qualifies when net recharge exceeds 10 mm, the cluster-mean water table rises by more than 5 mm, and the resulting event-level Sy falls within a plausibility window of 0.01--0.50. The spread in event counts is not a sampling imbalance: the net-recharge criterion is met in 139--146 months at every cluster, as it must be when all clusters share one climate record, and the rise criterion in 91--111, fewer beneath the canopy where recharge is suppressed. What separates the clusters is the plausibility ceiling, which discards 39--60% of the months clearing both criteria --- 60% at C5, which is why its event count is the lowest in the network; the 0.01 floor removes no events at any cluster. Because the ceiling censors only the upper tail, every event-median is biased low by an amount that scales with the censored fraction: removing the clip raises the medians by +0.08 (C1) to +0.25 (C5), into a range of 0.29--0.61 that exceeds the drainable porosity of dune sand. The ceiling is therefore doing real work rather than trimming noise, but the correction it applies is not uniform across clusters, and at C5 the unclipped median (0.605) sits above the ceiling itself, so that cluster\'s estimate is set by the limit rather than by its own distribution. Uncorrected median values range from 0.210 (C1 Lake Edge) to 0.355 (C5 Coastal Forest), with broad interquartile ranges reflecting the inherent noise in monthly cluster-mean data. The two forested clusters return uncorrected medians (C4: 0.312, C5: 0.355) that sit at or above the open dune range (0.210--0.328): the WTF method attributes the full rainfall to recharge when 24% is intercepted, inflating the apparent Sy. After applying the interception correction of 24% of P (Freeman, 2008), the forested cluster medians fall to 0.260 (C4) and 0.326 (C5): C4 falls cleanly within the open dune range (0.210--0.328), while C5 sits at its upper edge. The C5 estimate is the least reliable in the network --- a majority of its rising-limb events return event-level Sy at or above the 0.50 plausibility ceiling (Section 3.7.3), so its median is constrained by that limit rather than freely estimated, and its modest apparent response to the interception correction is partly an artefact of the clip; it is therefore reported as a weak corroborator. Within this corrected dataset, a secondary pattern is visible: the two clusters with the lowest corrected Sy --- C1 (Lake Edge; 0.210) and C4 (Main Forest; 0.260) --- return lower values than C3 (Western Residual; 0.328) and C5 (Coastal Forest; 0.326), with C2 (Dune; 0.269) intermediate (Section 5.1). The pattern recurs in the per-well β₂ regression (Section 4.9.4) where elevation --- reflecting both vadose zone thickness and proximity to buried bedrock --- explains 97% of within-forest β₂ variance.

Qualifying events satisfy Δh \> 5 mm, net recharge \> 10 mm and the plausibility window 0.01 \< Sy \< 0.50; the number of qualifying events (n) and the fraction removed by the 0.50 ceiling are given beneath each cluster. The ceiling censors the upper tail only, so each median is biased low by an amount that scales with the censored fraction --- from 39% at C1 to 60% at C5, whose distribution is truncated hard against the limit. (Source: 17_wtf_03_event_boxplot.png).

An independent cross-check on these estimates is available from a second WTF method: an ordinary-least-squares regression of winter water-table rise on net recharge, which returns a per-cluster Sy from the regression slope (Table 8, OLS-winter column). The OLS estimates run higher than the event-medians at four of the five clusters (mean ratio 1.18), consistent with the documented tendency of WTF methods to bias high on absolute magnitude; the OLS values, like the event-medians, should be read as upper bounds rather than point estimates. The two methods agree on the principal spatial pattern --- both place the deep-sand Western Residual (C3) and Coastal Forest (C5) clusters at the high-storage end of the network. They diverge at two clusters, and the divergence is itself informative. At C1 (Lake Edge), the OLS regression returns the weakest fit of the five clusters (R² = 0.59, with C2 next-weakest at 0.67 and C3--C5 at 0.84--0.86), so the OLS estimate is least reliable where it disagrees; the event-median\'s placement of C1 as the low-storage end-member is retained. At C4 (Main Forest), the uncorrected OLS estimate ranks the cluster lowest in the network; the interception-corrected event-median is the estimate carried forward. Across both methods, the event-based median is retained as the primary specific-yield estimate for each cluster; the OLS regression serves as a corroborating check on the spatial pattern.

A third, independent WTF estimator --- the rapid-recharge-event method of Crosbie et al. (2005; Section 3.7.3) --- provides a further check that shares the assumptions of neither the event-median nor the winter-OLS estimate. Selecting only short, sharply-rising episodes in which drainage during the rise is negligible, it returns cluster median Sy values of 0.180 (C1, 95% CI \[0.097, 0.220\], n = 19), 0.260 (C2, \[0.180, 0.333\], n = 20), 0.319 (C3, \[0.274, 0.409\], n = 16), 0.306 (C4, interception-corrected, \[0.245, 0.360\], n = 13) and 0.311 (C5, interception-corrected, \[0.270, 0.376\], n = 13). At C3 (Western Residual) all three methods agree within 0.054 (0.328, 0.319 and 0.373), so the high-storage placement of the deep-sand cluster is robust to estimator choice. At C1 (Lake Edge) the rapid-event estimate (0.180) sits with the event-median (0.210) well below the winter-OLS value (0.348); the low-storage placement of C1 is retained on the agreement of the two drainage-insensitive estimators. The coarse specific-yield gradient across the network is therefore consistent across three methodologically distinct estimators, while the fine ordering at the high-storage end (C3 versus C5) remains method-dependent --- the winter-OLS placing C5 highest, the two event-based methods placing C3 highest --- and all three, as noted, are upper bounds on effective storage rather than point estimates.

Individual well Sy values underlying the spatial mapping of Figure 13 are considered separately below. All five WTF medians exceed the literature specific yields for unconfined dune sand and, at C1, glacial till (C1: 0.08; C2--C5: 0.12; Fetter, 2001) --- benchmark values, not inputs to the Sy-free water balance of Section 4.2.3 --- by a factor of two to three, consistent with the known tendency of monthly WTF to conflate gravity drainage with capillary fringe release (Healy and Cook, 2002; Scanlon et al., 2002). The WTF estimates should therefore be interpreted as upper bounds on effective storage. Direct field measurement by slug test or pumping test at representative wells per cluster is identified as a priority for future work.

The well-level analysis is presented here for its spatial content rather than as a competing storage estimate. ## []{#anchor-9}Checking the Clusters: Pearson Affinity Analysis

Of the 66 wells in the reference network, 63 confirmed their primary cluster membership through the Pearson Affinity Analysis (Section 3.3). Membership is characterized by three distinct tiers based on the correlation delta (Δr) between assigned and neighbouring cluster centroids: Core members (17 wells) with an unambiguous dominant affinity to their assigned cluster (Δr \> 0.05), representing stable hydrogeological anchors within their designated geomorphological zone; Fuzzy members (46 wells) exhibiting closely competing affinities between their primary and secondary clusters (Δr \< 0.05), identifying areas where the groundwater regime transitions smoothly between adjacent structural blocks; and three Spy classifications where the well\'s highest temporal affinity belongs to a different cluster than Ward\'s assignment. CEH21 and CEH4 (both assigned C3 Western Residual) show strongest affinity with C5 Coastal Forest, consistent with their coastal-margin position where the Western Residual and Coastal Forest signatures overlap; NW13 (assigned C3) shows strongest affinity with C2 Dune. All three Spy deltas are small (\|Δr\| \< 0.012): borderline assignments at gradational boundaries.

Classification confidence was further characterized by the Multi-Cluster Affinity flag, raised where three or more cluster centroids achieved a correlation of r \> 0.90. This criterion was met at 46 of 66 wells, reflecting the high mutual correlation among the five cluster centroids in a contiguous, highly transmissive sand aquifer. The count measures how much of each hydrograph the clusters share --- the rainfall signal every well carries --- and not how well they are separated: the partition is on the shape of the response once that shared signal is removed, which is what the correlation distance of Section 3.2.1 measures and what the bootstrap stability below confirms, and the covariate test of Section 3.2 shows the labels carry drainage and atmospheric-draw structure that position and land cover do not. Of these, 21 are concentrated within the gradational C1/C2/C3 transitional zone of the mid-eastern dune sector, 14 lie along the C2/C3/C5 boundary where the Dune, Western Residual and Coastal Forest signatures converge, and 9 lie along the C3/C4/C5 forest--dune boundary, and 2 lie along the C2/C3/C4 boundary. The MCA flags identify the locations of greatest structural ambiguity within the network (Figure 15a).

The extended network analysis (Section 3.3.3) classified all 22 extended wells against the reference centroids, yielding 3 Ext_Core and 19 Ext_Fuzzy assignments (Figure 15b). With less temporal overlap against the centroid time series, affinity margins are compressed, which is why Fuzzy classifications predominate.

Within the extended network, the clearfell treatment wells showed mixed affinities across the C3/C4/C5 boundary, with all wells carrying Multi-Cluster Affinity flags (r \> 0.90 with three or more centroids). FE1 and LIS1 returned strongest affinity with C4 Main Forest (r = 0.989 and 0.973 respectively), while FE2 and FE4 showed marginally strongest affinity with C5 Coastal Forest (r = 0.975 and 0.972) with C4 within 0.006. FE3 showed strongest affinity with C5 (r = 0.985) followed by C3 (r = 0.974). WMC3, in the reference network, showed strongest affinity with C3 (r = 0.965) with C5 a close second (r = 0.961). The affinity profiles for these and the other selected wells are plotted in Figure 14. The small deltas (Δr = 0.003--0.037) place the clearfell zone at the gradational boundary between the Western Residual, Main Forest and Coastal Forest clusters. Forest-range affinities (C4 or C5) persist at these wells despite the December 2017 clearfell (Section 5.1.1).

## []{#anchor-10}Model Benchmarking: State-Space Model Comparison with Traditional Linear Models

The SSM was compared to a TLM as outlined in Section 3.4.2. In one-step diagnostic mode --- where each prediction is corrected with the observed water level from the previous month --- both models track the observed record almost identically (median R² 0.91 and 0.92 respectively; Table 9). The difference emerges under autonomous simulation. Over 100 months without observational correction, the TLM diverges rapidly at wells with strong head-dependent drainage (e.g. CEH6, C1 Lake Edge: TLM NSE = −1.89, SSM NSE = +0.67; Figure 16), while the SSM maintains physical consistency through its storage decay term. Across the full 66-well reference network, the SSM achieves a median iterative NSE of 0.72 compared with −0.03 for the TLM --- a median gain of +0.82 NSE units --- and returns a positive iterative NSE at 65 of 66 wells compared with 30 of 66 for the TLM (Table 9). The improvement varies systematically across the five clusters (Figure 17a, 16b): C1 Lake Edge shows the largest median gain (+1.524), ; C2 (+0.909), C3 (+0.623) and C5 (+0.499) show substantial gains; and C4 Main Forest shows the smallest (+0.410), where β₃ is lowest (0.018; Section 5.2.4). The sole well where the SSM fails is CEH14 (C4, iterative NSE = −6.42), a ridge-flank well (Section 5.2.3). Spatial visualization (Figure 17) shows the same pattern geographically, with the largest gains concentrated along the forest--Warren boundary and the C1 lake-buffer sector.

The depth-dependent PET grid search (Section 3.7.1) provides an independent diagnostic of how completely the standard fixed-β₂ formulation captures the atmospheric draw signal. The grid search produced statistically significant NSE improvement at all five clusters, where κ (m⁻¹) is the exponential decay rate controlling how rapidly the PET signal attenuates with water table depth: C1 (ΔNSE = +0.184, κ = 2.25 m⁻¹), C4 (+0.134, κ = 0.20), C2 (+0.094, κ = 0.95), C3 (+0.043, κ = 0.45) and C5 (+0.033, κ = 0.50). AIC improvement is decisive at every cluster. The fitted κ values correspond to 1/e decay depths of 0.44 m at C1 and 5.0 m at C4; their interpretation is developed in Sections 5.2.2 and 5.6.1.

## []{#anchor-11}Dune Scraping Intervention Analysis

### []{#anchor-12}**Background Environmental Drift**

Three dipwells within the dune slack system --- CEH36, CEH18 and CEH21 --- were subject to ground surface lowering by mechanical scraping, with CEH36 scraped in April 2015 and CEH18 and CEH21 scraped in October 2023. The analysis uses a two-tier CUSUM-BACI framework (Section 3.5) to isolate the scraping signal from background environmental drift, with CEH4 and CEH22 serving as paired controls. Tier 1 analysis at CEH4 and CEH22 both show accelerating negative CUSUM trajectories across the monitoring period, reaching −10.55 m and −19.02 m respectively by early 2026 (Section 3.5.3; Figure 18). Both controls --- CEH22 and CEH4 near the coast --- deteriorate independently of any management action (Section 5.4.3). CEH22\'s trajectory is the more severe, accelerating markedly from 2021 onwards.

![**Figure : **Tier 1 background environmental drift analysis. CUSUM time series for control wells CEH4 (left) and CEH22 (right) decomposed by management era relative to the regional mean. Upper panels show monthly Δ water level (treatment well minus regional mean) with era mean levels indicated by dashed horizontal lines. Lower panels show cumulative CUSUM trajectories. A rising CUSUM indicates the well is performing above the regional mean (shallower water table); a falling CUSUM indicates below-average performance (deeper water table). The accelerating negative CUSUM at both control wells confirms a system-wide deterioration trend independent of local management interventions. (Source: 09_scrape_05_tier1_background_drift.png)](Pictures/100000010000076A000005D7F202093E.png "fig:"){width="6.211in" height="4.9429in"}

CEH4 shows an additional deterioration from December 2017 onwards, superimposed on and inseparable from its longer-run trend. These Tier 1 trajectories establish that both local controls are experiencing substantial background decline that must be accounted for before any scraping benefit can be assessed.

### []{#anchor-13}Paired BACI and Robustness

In this context, Tier 2 paired analysis shows a modest positive signal at CEH36 during the Pure Scraping era (April 2015 to December 2017), the only well and era combination to show a net benefit after Tier 1 correction. Three independent methods all return a positive scraping benefit: the two control-differenced methods agree closely --- raw BACI vs CEH4 (+0.129 m) and synthetic control from 11 donor wells (+0.137 m) --- while the SSM forward residual, an autonomous-forecast estimator and the most conservative of the three, is lower at +0.081 m (Figure 19). The cumulative CUSUM for CEH36 rises strongly from 2018 onwards, as CEH4 deteriorates; the synthetic control separates the scraping signal from CEH4\'s own trajectory (Figure 20). CEH18 sits consistently negative relative to CEH4 throughout the full record including the pre-scraping baseline; only a modest recovery is visible after the October 2023 scraping. CEH21\'s rising CUSUM from 2022 onwards is read against a control, CEH22, that is itself deteriorating (Section 4.5.1), which inflates the apparent relative improvement; these results are noted for completeness only.

After Tier 1 correction for background drift, the net benefit at CEH36 reversed to −0.049 m during the Felling Pulse era, as the coastal erosion signal in CEH4 --- compounded from 2018 by the secondary clearfell pulse --- progressively eroded the scraping gain. The raw Tier 2 CUSUM tells a different story, with CEH36 rising strongly relative to CEH4 through this period --- but as established above, this reflects CEH4\'s own deterioration rather than genuine improvement at CEH36. At CEH18 and CEH21, scraped in October 2023, no scraping-specific response survived Tier 1 correction for background drift. CEH18\'s corrected net benefit was −0.073 m after scraping; CEH21\'s paired control (CEH22) is itself on a coastal erosion trajectory, so a net benefit cannot be reliably estimated. The monitoring window for both wells is short (two post-scraping summers) and the analysis is likely underpowered to detect benefits of the magnitude observed at CEH36.

The annual summer minimum records for all three treatment wells, partitioned by management era and plotted against the Curreli et al. (2013) ecological thresholds, are presented in Figure 22. The progressive deepening of the CEH4 control well across all eras --- from 1.16 m at baseline to 1.18 m during the Pure Scraping era and 1.40 m during the Felling Pulse --- is consistent with the system-wide climate drying trend documented in Section 4.8.1 and confirms that management benefit must be assessed against this background trajectory rather than in absolute terms.

### []{#anchor-15}**Summer Minima**

**The annual summer minimum depth records for the three scraping treatment wells and the CEH4 control well, partitioned by management era, are shown in Figure 22. CEH36 shows a clear reduction in summer minimum depth during the Pure Scraping era (April 2015 to December 2017), with the era mean shallowing from −1.115 m (pre-scraping, n = 4 summers) to −0.917 m (2015--17, n = 3 summers) --- a raw improvement of 198 mm (Figure 22). The era mean is −0.986 m in the post-felling era. Neither CEH18 nor CEH21 shows a clearly established summer minimum response to the October 2023 scraping --- the post-rescrape record comprises only two summers with high inter-annual variability, and CEH21\'s apparent improvement does not survive background correction against CEH22. The CEH4 control well deepens progressively across all eras (−1.075 m pre-scraping to −1.148 m during the Felling Pulse).**

**The paired BACI summer minima analysis (09c) confirms the scraping benefit at CEH36 is statistically significant against the paired control CEH4 (+195 mm, p = 0.00**4**) and also significant against the climate control centroid (+161 mm, p = 0.006). Neither CEH18 (+56 mm, p = 0.20) nor CEH21 (−8 mm, p = 0.89) showed significant paired shifts... CEH4 showed a non-significant change against the climate centroid (−34 mm, p = 0.33); the background drying trajectory is evidenced instead by the Tier-1 CUSUM decline and the era-mean progression (Section 4.5.1) (Figures 23, 24) and, in climate-corrected anomaly terms, by the divergence of the two wells after April 2015 (Figure 25). The distributional view (Figure 34) confirms this pattern: Impact and Edge tier summer minima track the Forest Control trajectory without detectable divergence after felling, while the Coastal Control shows progressive deepening consistent with coastal erosion.**

**The same paired comparison on the five-year mean spring water level (MSL5; Section 4.8.3) corroborates the benefit on the baseline vegetation metric. MSL5 at CEH36 shallows from −0.72 m at window-end 2015 to approximately −0.50 m across window-ends 2017--2023, opening a sustained separation of roughly +0.05 to +0.10 m from the paired control CEH4 --- which itself holds near −0.60 m and deepens late in the record under the coastal-erosion and drying trajectory. Because MSL5 is a rolling five-year mean, the scraping signal enters the metric gradually as post-scrape springs populate the window rather than as a discrete step, and part of the 2015--2017 shallowing is shared with CEH4 as the wet springs of that period enter both wells\' windows; the sustained CEH36-minus-CEH4 separation that persists through the post-scrape record is, however, consistent in direction and approximate magnitude with the +195 mm paired summer-minimum benefit (Figure 24) and the +129 mm BACI-corrected monthly benefit (Section 4.5.2). The benefit is thus present on all three metrics --- the monthly mean, the summer minimum and the five-year spring baseline (Section 5.4.1).**

### []{#anchor-16}**Scraping Propagation into the Surrounding Aquifer**

**A supplementary analysis tested whether the CEH36 scraping signal propagated uphill into the surrounding aquifer, comparing split-window SSM fits at ten wells between 250 m and 780 m from CEH36, with BACI correction against seven distant C3 control wells. Under a full three-coefficient refit, all eight wells within 575 m returned a positive BACI-corrected change in the drainage coefficient (mean Δβ₃ = +5.0 × 10⁻³; one-sample t = 4.98, p = 0.002). Its interpretation is in Section 5.4.3.**

The uphill wells traverse pre-existing spatial gradients in the drainage coefficient. The wells nearer CEH36 lie within the C3 Western Residual cluster, which carries a significant internal β₃ gradient along the south-west to north-east axis (Section 4.9.2; β₃ increasing inland, r = +0.58, p = 0.006); the higher uphill wells lie within the C4 and C5 forest zone, where β₃ shows a significant elevation dependence (Section 4.9.4; r = −0.77, p = 0.001). The BACI-corrected Δβ₃ shows no decay with distance from CEH36.

The aquifer diffusivity timescale L_B²Sy/(Kb) exceeds seven years at a separation of 570 m (Fetter, 2001), against a 31-month post-scraping record. The inferred ground surface lowering at CEH36 is approximately 0.42 m (back-calculated as d_ex = H₀/Sy from the measured BACI step H₀ ≈ 0.13 m and open-dune Sy ≈ 0.31; Figure 26); the water-table shallowing partially re-equilibrates over approximately two years, retaining +129 mm as the BACI-corrected benefit during the pure scraping era (Section 4.5.2). The SSM forward residual analysis (Figure 20b) shows near-zero deviation during this period.

The localized response at CEH36 and absence of a spatial gradient uphill at well distances of 850--1100 m within the 31-month observation window are consistent with the scraping effect being either spatially confined or propagating on timescales longer than the available record (Section 5.4.3). ### []{#anchor-17}**Scenario Contextualization**

> To contextualize the observed scraping benefit at CEH36, five alternative interventions were compared at the same well under two climate forcings (09d). Under annual-mean forcing (Figure 27), the observed scraping benefit (+46.4 mm w.e./month) exceeds each alternative: clearfell +16.7, thinning +8.3, broadleaf +5.1, and climate wet +7.9 mm/month, against −14.1 mm/month under climate dry. Evaluated under summer forcing (Figure 28) the ranking is unchanged and the forestry gains are marginally smaller (clearfell +14.9, thinning +7.4, broadleaf +3.6), while the climate-dry penalty is marginally larger (−14.4); both figures report the same equilibrium volumetric quantity and are directly comparable. Both figures also show the modelled off-site neighbour drawdown the scrape imposes on the surrounding water table (−31.2 mm w.e./month at 100 m, decaying to −16.1 at 250 m): scraping raises the slack locally but draws its neighbours down; the canopy-management scenarios carry no off-site term. The measured level fall at the nearest uphill well, WMC3, is in Section 4.6.3. (For reference, the observed paired-BACI summer-minimum shift at CEH36 was +195 mm; the equilibrium framework does not resolve summer minima, so it is not plotted.)

## []{#anchor-18}The December 2017 Experimental Clearfell: Monitoring and Retrospective Analysis

### []{#anchor-19}**Interpretive Context**

Three features of the monitoring record bear on interpretation of the clearfell results. First, wells within the clearfell footprint (FE1--FE4, LIS1) and the scraping treatment well CEH36 were excluded from the BACI design on the grounds of insufficient or confounded pre-felling baselines (Section 3.5.4). FE1 and FE2, which have approximately 28 months of pre-felling record but no pre-scraping baseline, were excluded from the primary BACI design because their late start dates create an unstable impact centroid when pooled with WMC3 --- the changing well composition introduces spurious level shifts that the ANCOVA conflates with the intervention steps. These wells were instead included as a robustness check via donor-regression synthetic extension, which provides a stable-composition centroid across all three eras (Section 4.6.7). Second, all clearfell analyses use the period from 2010 onwards as the effective baseline, because only three of nine C4 wells were operational before mid-2010 and these are unrepresentative of the cluster (Section 4.2.1). Third, the April 2015 scraping event at CEH36 produced a significant level shift 32 months before the clearfell; the ANCOVA\'s distance-weighted scraping covariate absorbs this, but the short pre-clearfell window encompasses only three summer minima, limiting baseline power.

### []{#anchor-20}**Climate Sensitivity**

The CWB × clearfell interaction was non-significant in the Forest control models (Impact p = 0.40, Edge p = 0.16), indicating that the rate at which the BACI gap responds to cumulative water balance deficit did not detectably change after felling when that response is modelled as a single linear slope. The relationship is shown in Figure 29: the fitted pre-felling and post-felling climate-response lines are effectively parallel, offset by the clearfell step (Section 4.6.3).

A linear slope is, however, a blunt instrument for the buffering hypothesis as it would most plausibly operate. If the canopy moderated the water table specifically against climate *extremes*, the effect would be concentrated at the wet or dry tails of the cumulative water balance range and could average close to zero across the full range, leaving a linear interaction undetectably small. To test this directly, a non-linear extension of the headline model was fitted, adding a centred CWB² term and a CWB² × clearfell interaction to the full ANCOVA specification. The extension does not support the hypothesis. The CWB² × clearfell interaction is negative at both zones --- the direction a dry-tail buffering effect would produce --- but reaches significance at neither (Impact −15.5 mm per (100 mm CWB)², p = 0.17; Edge −9.1 mm per (100 mm CWB)², p = 0.28). The joint F-test of the two added curvature terms is non-significant at Impact (p = 0.20) and marginal at Edge (p = 0.051), and the curvature model is not preferred over the linear one by AIC at Impact (ΔAIC +0.6); at Edge it is (ΔAIC −2.3). The CWB² main effect is non-significant at both zones. The negative interaction sign means the post-felling response is concave in cumulative water balance: the felling-attributable rise in the water table is larger in dry, low-water-balance conditions than in wet ones.

This is reported as a preliminary finding. It rests on a single interacted quadratic term and one felling event at one site, and it is a sensitivity variant only: the headline clearfell step and the linear ANCOVA model of Section 4.6.3 are unchanged. The clearfell\'s effect on the water table was concentrated in dry periods; the alternative explanations and the buffering reading are in Section 5.5.1.

The Climate-control models --- which contrast the felled wells against the unforested Western Block --- return non-significant CWB × clearfell interactions (Impact p = 0.55, Edge p = 0.28). The Forest-control comparison is the position-matched test and its results, linear and non-linear, are the headline findings; the Climate-control interactions are not interpreted as a clearfell-specific change in canopy water-balance physics.

**Table :** Three-counterfactual ANCOVA-BACI results for the December 2017 clearfell. Each row reports the clearfell step estimate from a separate ANCOVA model fitted to the monthly BACI gap (target tier centroid minus control centroid). Covariates: centred cumulative water balance (CWB), distance-weighted scraping dummy (L_s = 300 m), CWB × clearfell interaction, and coastal-drift term. The Forest control is the most direct test of the clearfell hypothesis: it compares felled wells against unfelled forest sharing the same canopy and substrate, isolating the felling response from the coastal erosion gradient. All comparisons use a record-length-balanced window beginning January 2011 --- the date from which every well in the five-tier comparison network has continuous record. The control centroid is computed on a fixed-membership basis: a month enters the BACI series only when every control-roster well has a reading, so the centroid is not silently re-weighted by control wells going offline mid-record (clearfell_common v1.7.0). Sample sizes therefore differ between comparisons. (Source: 10a_01_ancova_comparison_table.csv)

**

Against the Forest control, the clearfell step was +113 mm for Impact (p = 0.002) and +30 mm for Edge (p = 0.25) (Figure 31, Figure 32). The Impact step is statistically significant; the Edge step is not. Against the Climate control, the clearfell step was −15 mm for Impact (p = 0.56) and −107 mm for Edge (p \< 0.001). Against the Combined control, the clearfell step was +70 mm for Impact (p \< 0.001) and −20 mm for Edge (p = 0.13). The interpretation of the contrasting Forest, Climate and Combined results is taken up in Section 5.

The scraping covariate was significant in both Forest-control models: +324 mm at Impact (p = 0.004) and +568 mm at Edge (p \< 0.001). Sensitivity analysis across three decay length scales (L_s = 200, 300, 500 m) produced consistent clearfell coefficients, so the scraping and clearfell terms are temporally well-separated. These covariate coefficients index the temporal separation of the two interventions in the model; they are not a physical estimate of the scraping effect on the impact well. In the raw, uncorrected BACI gap the two scraping events each *lower* the WMC3-minus-forest-control level, whereas the climate-corrected covariate carries the opposite sign because it is estimated jointly with the cumulative-water-balance and coastal-drift terms. Figure 30 shows the raw gap and its per-era steps directly.

The raw before-and-after evidence for all three interventions is shown in Figure 30. In the uncorrected WMC3-minus-forest-control gap, the December 2017 clearfell registers a +41 mm difference-in-differences step --- the raw counterpart to the +113 mm climate-corrected ANCOVA step above, the two differing because the raw step retains the drier-than-average pre-felling climate the ANCOVA removes. The gap also steps downward at each scraping event, by a near-identical amount (−55 mm in 2015, −54 mm in 2023). WMC3 lies 262 m from CEH36, and in Section 4.5.5 it returned an essentially zero BACI-corrected Δβ₃: the level steps while the drainage coefficient does not (Section 5.4.1). The fitted drainage half-life (ln 2 / β₃) is 13--21 months at the wells within \~400 m of the scrape, against a 31-month post-scraping window. The 2015 drawdown is the same scraping signal that confounds the pre-felling baseline of the surrounding within-footprint wells; WMC3 alone has a pre-2015 record that lets the scraping step be separated, which is why it is retained as the sole impact well while CEH36 and the FE wells are excluded (Section 4.6.1). The steps remain uncorrected for differential climate sensitivity between WMC3 and the forest control, so they are presented as consistent with scraping drawdown rather than as a confirmed magnitude.

The coastal-drift covariate in Table 11\'s ANCOVA design absorbs progressive divergence between impact and control wells across the post-felling era, and Table 12 reports the differential each contrast absorbs. The covariate is the fitted coastal profile of Section 4.10.2, evaluated at each tier\'s mean distance from the shore and differenced between target and control, so its coefficient ξ is the fraction of that field the contrast feels and ξ = 1 is exactly the amplitude fitted network-wide. What the covariate does is keep that drift from being attributed to the felling step, which is the use made of it in Section 4.6.3; the residual coastal-retreat decline it absorbs is discussed in Section 5.5.

**Table : ** The coastal-drift term fitted in each ANCOVA contrast (Section 4.6.3). ξ is the amplitude of the network-scale coastal gradient that each target-minus-control contrast feels, and is dimensionless: ξ = 1 is exactly the field fitted independently in Section 4.10.2. The absorbed differential is ξ × the tier\'s coastal differential (mm yr⁻¹), with ±1 SE propagated from the coefficient SE. Because the covariate is the fitted gradient field itself, the comparison with the model prediction is an internal consistency check rather than independent corroboration: it asks, in effect, whether ξ = 1. It is a drift control, not a measurement of a spatial gradient. (Source: 25_04_baci_corroboration.csv)

******

****Four-zone pooled-panel cross-check.**** The three-counterfactual ANCOVA above fits the felling step six times --- once per (control, zone) pair --- and each fit has its own dependent variable, because the BACI gap is the target centroid minus a control centroid and the control centroid differs between the Forest, Climate and Combined configurations. The six steps therefore do not share a covariance matrix and are not subtractable. As a cross-check, a four-zone pooled-panel model (Script 10k) was fitted: the Forest control, a second western-dune control (C3/Warren), the Edge tier and the Impact well are stacked into one long-form panel, and every zone contrast is read off a single internally-consistent joint fit. This supplements, and does not replace, the three-counterfactual ANCOVA, which remains the principal clearfell analysis.****

The joint fit returns three primary zone-versus-Forest monthly contrasts: Impact−Forest +0.024 m (95% CI \[+0.001, +0.047\], p = 0.043), Edge−Forest −0.039 m (p = 0.064, ns), and C3/Warren−Forest +0.009 m (p = 0.485, ns); joint model R² = 0.848, N = 2489 well-months. The four-zone result is consistent with the principal analysis. The joint-fit Impact−Forest step (+0.024 m) is smaller in magnitude than the three-counterfactual Forest × Impact step (+0.113 m); the two estimators partition climate variance differently --- the joint panel estimates climate sensitivity from the full cross-zone monthly record, so a portion of the monthly variance the separately-fitted ANCOVA attributes to the felling step is attributed to climate in the joint fit. The felling response is positive and statistically significant under both estimators, and only the magnitude is sensitive to the partitioning choice. Dropping the easting × time covariate moves the joint-fit Impact step only from +0.024 m to +0.026 m, significance unchanged.

The Impact−Edge difference of +0.063 m is an exact arithmetic combination of two primary contrasts; its standard error is covariance-dependent and not comparable to a primary contrast, so it is not cited with a p-value here. It is instead corroborated independently by the two-zone Impact-versus-Edge estimator (Script 10j), which returns a monthly Impact−Edge step of +0.065 m (p = 0.0003) --- the close agreement between the two estimators is the warrant for the contrast.

### []{#anchor-22}**Summer Minima**

The annual summer minimum depth (June--September) --- the ecologically critical metric determining dune slack habitat viability (Curreli et al. 2013) --- was analysed for each well in the 17-well network. Four complementary analyses are reported: per-well Welch t-tests on the annual summer-minimum gap (Table 13); a mixed-effects model pooling within-tier (Table 14); a directly-fitted Jun--Sep ANCOVA on monthly observations, using the same three-counterfactual specification as the annual analysis (Section 3.5.4) restricted to the June--September window; and a four-zone pooled-panel cross-check fitted on the annual summer-minimum series (Section 3.5.4). The two ANCOVA-based analyses differ in estimator and in unit of observation: the Jun--Sep ANCOVA estimates the felling step from monthly observations as a differenced centroid, while the four-zone model estimates every zone contrast from a single joint fit on annual summer-minimum well-years --- the annual deepest point rather than the summer-window mean.

**Per-well summer-minimum shifts.** Pre- vs post-felling Welch t-tests on the annual summer-minimum gap (well minus Forest control centroid) found no significant clearfell effect at any well in the Impact or Edge tier (Table 13). The Impact well WMC3 showed a shift of −7 mm (p = 0.91). Individual Edge well shifts ranged from −9 mm at CEH30 to −97 mm at CEH16, all non-significant.

**

**Directly-fitted Jun--Sep ANCOVA.** A directly-fitted summer-window ANCOVA was run on the same five-tier specification as the annual analysis (Section 3.5), restricted to June--September observations (n = 52 months). Against the Forest control, the Jun--Sep clearfell step at the Impact tier was +46 mm (95% CI \[−69, +162\], p = 0.44), with R² = 0.34. A sensitivity variant dropping the CWB covariate and the CWB × clearfell interaction from the design matrix produced an estimate of +123 mm (95% CI \[−1, +247\], p = 0.06), with R² = 0.10. The contrast between the full-specification and CWB-dropped estimates is discussed in Section 5.

**Distributional comparison.** Figure 34 shows the distribution of summer minima across the five BACI tiers across three phases: pre-scraping baseline (2007 to April 2015), the 2015--17 era, and post-felling 2018 onwards. The Forest Control group shows stable summer minima throughout. The Impact and Edge tiers track the Forest Control trajectory across the three phases. The Coastal Control tier (CEH19, CEH17) shows progressive deepening across all three phases.

**Four-zone pooled-panel cross-check (summer minimum).** Whereas the directly-fitted Jun--Sep ANCOVA above estimates the felling step from monthly observations in the Jun--Sep window as a differenced centroid, the four-zone pooled-panel model (Section 3.5.4) estimates every zone contrast from a single joint fit on the annual summer-minimum series (Script 10l) --- the annual deepest point rather than the summer-window mean. The three primary zone-versus-Forest contrasts were Impact−Forest −7 mm (95% CI \[−23, +8\], p = 0.36), Edge−Forest −29 mm (p = 0.16) and C3/Warren−Forest +12 mm (p = 0.26); joint model R² = 0.724, N = 181 well-years. No zone contrast resolves a significant differential felling response at the summer minimum.

The four summer-window analyses converge: the per-well Welch tests, the pooled mixed-effects model, the directly-fitted Jun--Sep ANCOVA and the four-zone pooled-panel cross-check all return non-significant clearfell steps at the Impact and Edge tiers. The felling produced a measurable rise in the felled compartment\'s monthly-mean water table (Section 4.6.3) but no detectable change at the summer minimum --- the driest and most ecologically critical point of the year, and the level against which the Curreli SD15b and SD16 slack thresholds are defined.

Five-year mean spring water level. The same absence of a discrete felling response is seen in the five-year mean spring water level (MSL5; Section 4.8.3), the baseline metric most directly tied to dune-slack vegetation (van Willegen et al. 2025). At the Impact well WMC3, MSL5 carried no step at the December 2017 felling: the window-end values deepen through the post-felling years (−1.00 m at window-end 2018, −1.12 m at 2019, holding near −1.05 m through 2023) before recovering to −0.90 m at window-end 2024. The four Edge wells (CEH16, CEH20, CEH30, CEH31) show the same pattern --- flat to slightly deepening from 2018 to 2023, then a recovery first appearing at window-end 2024. The 2024 recovery is not clearfell-attributable: it appears synchronously across the felled wells, the unfelled Forest control, and every other cluster in the network (Section 4.8.3, Figure 44), six years after the intervention, and reflects the 2023--24 hydrological year entering the rolling five-year window rather than a delayed canopy-removal response. On the baseline metric, as on the summer minimum, the clearfell produced no detectable step against the background climate signal (Figure 33 shows the summer-minimum result by tier). The mean-monthly recovery established by the ANCOVA (Section 4.6.3) is thus specific to the monthly-mean level; it is not expressed in either of the two ecologically referenced metrics --- the summer minimum or the five-year spring baseline --- against which dune-slack viability is assessed.

### []{#anchor-23}**Spatial Step-Change Maps**

Climate-corrected step-change maps for the clearfell era are shown in Figure 35. Each well\'s step is computed relative to its own pre-intervention mean, corrected by subtracting the C3 open-dune control centroid step to remove the background climate signal. This correction removes shared climate forcing but does not account for the coastal erosion gradient, which produces a systematic east--west trend in the corrected steps. The map shows spatially uniform changes with no clear distance-decay from the felling compartment (Figure 35). The transect analysis confirms the absence of a distance gradient (Figure 37). The ANCOVA (Section 4.6.3), which explicitly models the coastal-retreat gradient, provides a cleaner estimate of the clearfell-specific effect.

### **Coefficient Decomposition**

The SSM was fitted independently to Before (record-length-balanced pre-felling window) and After (felling to end of record) windows for each well in the 17-well network, yielding per-well coefficient shifts Δβ₁, Δβ₂ and Δβ₃ (Script 10e). This decomposition is a mechanistic diagnostic: it characterizes *which* SSM pathway --- recharge, atmospheric draw or drainage --- shifted between eras and in *what direction*. It is not an estimate of the clearfell magnitude; the clearfell magnitude is the BACI step reported in Section 4.6.3. The per-era fits use the canonical no-intercept SSM (Section 3.5), consistent with Script 03 and the master coefficient table.

β₁ (recharge) declined at most wells across all five tiers: mean Δβ₁ = −0.10 at Impact, −0.27 at Edge, −0.05 at Forest Control, −0.32 at Coastal Control and −0.13 at Climate Control. The network-mean shift across the seventeen-well BACI network is Δβ₁ = −0.16, a 5.8% reduction against a pre-felling network mean of 2.81. The decline is present at the unfelled Climate Control and Forest Control tiers as well as at the treatment tiers; its candidacy as a mechanism for the network-wide summer-minimum decline is taken up in Section 5.5.

β₂ (atmospheric draw) increased at the unfelled Forest-Control wells (mean Δβ₂ = +0.15) with no comparable rise at the non-forest tiers. Refitting β₂ on a common PET support across the two eras leaves the Forest-Control increase positive while the Climate-Control tier remains negative (Section 5.5.1). The Impact-tier β₂ shift (Δβ₂ = −0.28) is a single-well estimate lying within one standard error of zero and is not interpreted; Edge-tier shifts were near zero in the mean (−0.03) and incoherent in sign across wells.

β₃ (drainage) shifts were small and spatially incoherent across all tiers (mean Δβ₃ between −0.01 and 0.00 at every tier), consistent with no systematic change in the drainage pathway.

Individual wells departed from these tier means. Within the Forest Control, NW10 and CEH2 showed β₁ increases (Δβ₁ = +0.28 and +0.12) against a network of general decline. These departures are retained: the per-well era coefficients carry wide confidence intervals (Figure 36) and exclusion would not be justified on physical grounds.

The decomposition therefore identifies a site-wide recharge decline and a forest-maturation signal in atmospheric draw, but does not by itself isolate a clearfell-specific coefficient signature; the clearfell effect is quantified by the BACI analysis of Section 4.6.3.

### []{#anchor-24}**Robustness**

Three independent methods were applied to test whether a clearfell-specific signal could be detected once the ANCOVA assumptions were relaxed.

**SSM residual normalization.** The SSM was calibrated on the pre-felling record for each well and run forward iteratively into the post-felling era. The Impact well WMC3 showed a +56 mm normalized step --- its post-felling water table 56 mm above the pre-felling SSM prediction. The Forest Control wells drifted upward by a larger mean of +78 mm over the same period, so against the Forest-control drift the Impact-specific component is approximately −22 mm: the Impact well\'s upward residual is slightly smaller than the unfelled forest controls\', and this method does not isolate a positive clearfell-specific step.

**Synthetic control.** A synthetic counterfactual for WMC3 constructed from six optimally weighted donor wells showed an Impact step of +99 mm (p = 0.001); the corresponding Edge synthetic-control step was +41 mm (p = 0.22), non-significant. The synthetic-control and SSM-residual methods agree that WMC3\'s gross post-felling step is of order +50 to +100 mm; they differ on how much survives normalization against the unfelled forest controls, and neither, after that normalization, resolves a clearfell-specific step distinguishable from zero.

**Clearfell transect.** Step changes across a transect from the plantation interior to the felling core showed no significant spatial gradient (−0.4 mm per 100 m, p = 0.19). A distance-decay response would be strongest at WMC3 and diminish outward; the observed pattern is statistically uniform (Figure 37). The post-felling spread in the transect hydrographs is nonetheless visibly wider than pre-felling (Figure 37, panel a), with WMC3 consistently above the pack (Section 5.5).

**Synthetic FE-well extension.** FE1 and FE2 --- which sit inside or at the immediate edge of the clearfell compartment but lack pre-scraping baselines --- were extended backwards using OLS donor regression calibrated on Forest Control wells (calibration R² \> 0.99, RMSE 18--25 mm; Section 4.6.1). Against the Forest control, the centroid of WMC3 + FE2 produced a clearfell step of +97 mm (95% CI \[+38, +156\], p = 0.002, R² = 0.31), consistent with the WMC3-only ANCOVA estimate of +113 mm (Section 4.6.3). FE2\'s post-felling divergence from its own donor counterfactual was +28 mm (p \< 0.001), indicating a significant within-compartment response. Extending the centroid to WMC3 + FE1 + FE2 returned a Forest-control clearfell step of +80 mm (95% CI \[+34, +126\], p \< 0.001). FE1 sits approximately 20 m outside the felling boundary in standing forest, so including it attenuates the step magnitude --- from +113 mm (WMC3 alone) through +97 mm (WMC3 + FE2) to +80 mm --- but the within-compartment signal remains highly significant throughout.

### **Temporal decay of the clearfell step and the canopy setting**

The Forest-control clearfell step is not stationary across the record. Split at January 2021, the Impact-well recovery against the Forest control falls from +154 mm in the early era (December 2017 to December 2020) to +36 mm in the late era (January 2021 onward), no longer distinguishable from zero, while the Edge-tier contrast falls from +64 mm to −11 mm over the same split, and the Impact well remains significantly elevated relative to the Edge tier in both eras (+88 mm early, +52 mm late). The relaxation is not an artefact of the coastal-drift correction: refitting each contrast under the four drift treatments of Section 3.5.5 leaves the early step above the late step in every case (Impact +154 to +36 with the Script 25 field, +122 to −40 with no drift, and +122 to −40 with a free per-era slope), and the per-era treatment, the direct test of an accelerating retreat, widens the gap rather than closing it (Figure 39; 10a_13_era_split.csv).

The step is robust to the composition of the Forest control. Estimated against only the two control wells lying outside any 1998 replant block (CEH34 and CEH2) it is +114 mm, essentially the +113 mm headline, so the two controls lying inside a replant block do not inflate it; a contrast between the in-block pair (CEH32, CEH33) and the outside pair is flat and non-significant in both eras (−19 mm early, −8 mm late) (10a_12_control_subset_sensitivity.csv).

The canopy trajectories give the setting (Figure 38; Section 3.5.5). The felled compartment falls from a mature-conifer texture to about 0.14 of the reference at felling and is held there by grazing, reaching only 0.15 by 2020 and 0.37 by 2026: it does not regenerate. The three 1998 replant blocks rise from near-bare in 2006 (0.15, 0.36 and −0.05 relative to the mature-conifer reference) to 0.77 to 0.89 by 2020 and 1.05 to 1.44 by 2026 \-\-- a developing canopy across the study window, on a trend present whether or not the isolated 2026 frame is included. The pooled untouched-forest control drifts gently from 1.47 in 2006 to about 1.15 and is flat across the BACI window, remaining dense and above the reference: the control forest was neither felled nor heavily thinned. The broadleaf restock grew in by about 2012, and the vegetated warren sits near zero throughout, the open-dune end of the scale. The replant reads above the reference by 2026 because it is unthinned whereas the reference stand has been thinned.

## []{#anchor-25}**Critical Rainfall Threshold Forecasting - Predicting Winter flooding and Summer droughts**

### []{#anchor-26}**Mechanistic State-Space Equations**

The cluster-level state-space equations (Section 3.6.1) fitted without intercept produced statistically significant coefficients at all five clusters (all p \< 0.001 except the C4 drainage coefficient β₃, where p = 0.002). Model fit ranged from R² = 0.812 at Western Residual (C3) to R² = 0.683 at Coastal Forest (C5), with C5 the least well fit and C4 Main Forest mid-range (R² = 0.722; Section 5.2.4). The full coefficient values are reported in Section 4.2.2; note that the β coefficients used in the forecasting tool are expressed in m/mm rainfall, one thousand times smaller than the m/m values in Table 3.

### []{#anchor-27}**Seasonal Prediction Equations**

The prediction equations were fitted at hydrological-year resolution, one equation per cluster under the k = 5 partition (Table 16). The two predictor terms --- winter rainfall total (P_winter) and antecedent summer minimum (h_min) --- show a clear spatial partitioning of dominance across the site.

In the Eastern Block, winter rainfall is the dominant predictor. P_winter is significant at Lake Edge (p = 0.002) and Dune (p = 0.002), while h_min is non-significant in both (p = 0.780 and 0.575 respectively).

In the Western Residual and forest clusters, the pattern reverses. The antecedent summer minimum is the dominant predictor: Western Residual (p = 0.008, R² = 0.670), Forest (p \< 0.001, R² = 0.885) and Coastal Forest (p \< 0.001, R² = 0.873). Winter rainfall is non-significant at all three (p = 0.052, 0.924 and 0.338 respectively). The intercepts are significant at Forest (p = 0.030) and Coastal Forest (p = 0.005). The reading of both patterns is in Section 5.2.5.

Two individual coefficients require comment. The negative h_min coefficient at Lake Edge (−0.058) is not mechanistically meaningful given its non-significance; it is an artefact of the small sample (n = 19) and the dominance of P_winter in that cluster. The negative P_winter coefficient in the Forest cluster (−0.00006) reflects multicollinearity with h_min and should not be interpreted mechanistically.

### []{#anchor-29}**Spatial Distribution of P_flood and Flooding Status Across the Well Network**

Application of the cluster-level P_flood equations derived in Section 3.6.3 to each well in the 88 well classified network (66 reference wells with per-well SSM coefficients; 22 extended wells assigned cluster-level coefficients via the Pearson affinity audit of Section 3.3), using that well\'s observed mean summer minimum as h₀, produces a per-well critical rainfall threshold expressed as either millimetres of cumulative winter rainfall or as a dimensionless multiplier m_P = P_flood / Σ P_clim, where Σ P_clim is the long-term mean rainfall over the cluster-specific recharge horizon (400 mm for C1/C2 over Oct--Jan; 461 mm for C3/C4/C5 over Oct--Feb). A well with m_P = 1.0 would flood under an average winter; m_P \> 1.0 indicates that above-average rainfall is required. The network-wide picture is summarized in Figures 40--43.

The summer minimum depth map (Figure 40; Section 3.6.5) classifies each well against the five eco-hydrological bands derived from Curreli et al. (2013) and introduced in Section 2: SD15b wet slack viability (\<0.61 m), SD15b-recoverable (0.61--0.75 m), SD16 dry slack (0.75--0.98 m), SD16-recoverable (0.98--1.20 m), and beyond-recoverable (\>1.20 m). The two forest clusters (C4 and C5) show the deepest mean summer minima across the network, consistently below 0.98 m. Most C4 and C5 wells fall within the SD16 or beyond-recoverable zone. By contrast, the majority of C1 Lake Edge wells maintain mean summer minima within or close to the SD15b wet slack zone. Of the 88 wells in the classified network, 41 have mean summer minima deeper than 0.98 m --- the SD16 dry slack threshold --- of which 24 are below the SD16-recovery threshold of 1.20 m.

The P_flood map (Figure 41) quantifies the rainfall demand implied by these summer minima and reveals a progressive, cluster-ordered closure of the operational window (Table 18). Almost every well in the classified network requires winter rainfall above its climatological mean to reach the slack floor: 87 of the 88 wells have m_P \> 1.0, the single exception (m_P = 0.98) flooding marginally below an average winter. Under mildly wet winters ****(1.0 ≤ m_P \< 1.5), 59 wells (67%)**** become reachable; ****a further 24 (27%) require wet winters of varying rarity (1.5 ≤ m_P \< 2.5). The remaining 4 wells (5%) have m_P ≥ 2.5 --- they require at least 2.5 times the climatological mean winter rainfall, a total well beyond the wettest winter in the \~95-year RAF Valley record. For these wells the slack floor is not reachable under any winter rainfall yet observed: the wettest winter on record (745 mm in 2001, 1.51× the climatological mean) delivers only 60% of the m_P = 2.5 demand.****

The winter maximum depth map (Figure 42) shows that Eastern Block wells achieve the shallowest winter maxima. Western Residual and Forest wells rarely approach the 0 m threshold required by SD15b communities. The flooding frequency map (Figure 43) summarises the record as a frequency: C1 wells show the highest flooding frequency across the monitoring period; C3 wells show very low frequency; C4 and C5 Forest wells show essentially zero, with the water table failing to reach the ground surface in any monitored year.

### []{#anchor-30}Critical Rainfall Threshold Equations (P_flood)

The structural difference between clusters is immediately apparent from the threshold equations (Table 19; Section 3.6.3). The coefficients from Table 3, together with the cluster-specific recharge horizons from October to each cluster\'s historical peak month (four months for C1 and C2, five months for C3, C4 and C5) and the long-term monthly RAF Valley rainfall and PET climatology, propagate through the iterated closed form of Section 3.6.3 to produce a linear relationship between observed summer-minimum depth and required winter rainfall. The C4 recharge horizon endpoint is marginal --- the cluster\'s historical mean peak falls between February and March depending on the treatment of partial monitoring years --- and the shorter February horizon is adopted as the conservative choice; the C1, C2, C3 and C5 horizons are unambiguous.

The iterated derivation reduces to the form P_flood = A · d_w + B for each cluster, where d_w is the observed summer-minimum depth below ground (m, positive) and P_flood is the cumulative winter rainfall required over the cluster\'s recharge horizon (mm). The slope A represents the marginal rainfall demand per additional metre of summer drawdown, and the intercept B represents the rainfall demand required even for a well already at the surface --- non-zero because accumulated winter PET continues to draw down the water table through the recharge season. Both terms express the cluster gradient directly: A rises from 174 mm per metre at C1 through 214 (C2) and 238 (C3) to 362 (C5) and 383 (C4), and B ranges from 275 mm (C4) to 415 mm (C5).

As a worked example, at a typical C3 well with a mean summer minimum of 1.0 m below ground, P_flood = 237.59 × 1.0 + 365.47 = 603.1 mm of cumulative winter rainfall over the October--February recharge horizon, corresponding to a rainfall multiplier m_P = 603/461 = 1.31 times the long-term climatological total. The same depth at a C2 well produces P_flood = 214.10 × 1.0 + 289.56 = 503.7 mm (m_P = 504/400 = 1.26), a 99 mm difference reflecting the stronger antecedent-depth dependence and longer recharge horizon of C3. The C2 well lies within the marginally-wet-winter band; the C3 well requires wetter conditions over a longer accumulation of months.

  C2        Dune               Oct--Jan (4 mo)   214.11·d_w + 289.56     400
  C3        Western Residual   Oct--Feb (5 mo)   237.59·d_w + 365.47     461
  C4        Main Forest        Oct--Feb (5 mo)   383.49·d_w + 274.93     461
