**Table : **Cluster-specific linear forms derived from the iterated closed-form P_flood solution of Section 3.6.3, reduced by substituting fitted SSM coefficients (β₁, β₂, β₃), cluster recharge horizons (n = 4 for C1/C2, 5 for C3/C4/C5), and RAF Valley long-term monthly rainfall and PET climatology (2005--2026). Input variable d_w is the observed mean summer minimum water table depth below ground in metres, entered as a positive number (e.g. d_w = 1.26 for a water table 1.26 m below the surface). Output P_flood is the cumulative rainfall (mm) required over the cluster\'s recharge horizon (October to the historical mean peak month) to raise the water table to the slack floor (h_target = 0 m), assuming monthly rainfall scales uniformly by a multiplier m_P and monthly PET follows climatological means. The rainfall multiplier is m_P = P_flood / Σ P̄ᵢ; values above 1.0 indicate rainfall above the climatological mean is required. (Source: 11_forecast_pflood_summary.csv).

## []{#anchor-31}**Climate Trajectory and Threshold Exceedance**

****The spatial distribution of mean annual summer minima and winter maxima across the full dipwell network is presented in Figures 40 and 42 respectively, classified against the Curreli et al. (2013) eco-hydrological thresholds introduced in Section 2. The cluster-level trajectories and threshold exceedance analysis presented in this section quantify the rate and direction of change over the 21-year monitoring period.****

### []{#anchor-32}**Summer and Winter Trajectories**

Summer minimum trends were fitted for all five clusters over the monitoring period (Section 3.6.4; Figure 46, panel a). All clusters show declining summer minima, although the rates and significance levels vary substantially. C1 Lake Edge declined at −0.0109 m yr⁻¹ (R² = 0.234, p = 0.031, n = 20) and C5 Coastal Forest at −0.0359 m yr⁻¹ (R² = 0.394, p = 0.003, n = 20) --- the only two clusters reaching statistical significance at the 5% level. C2 Dune was marginal (−0.0112 m yr⁻¹, p = 0.071, n = 21). C3 Western Residual (−0.0094 m yr⁻¹, p = 0.188) and C4 Main Forest (−0.0178 m yr⁻¹, p = 0.232) were non-significant.

A bootstrap of the C1 summer-minimum trend (Figure 47; n = 1000 year-resampling replicates of the OLS fit) places the median crossing year of the SD16 dry-slack viability threshold at 2028, with a 90% confidence interval of 2022--2049; the interval is wide because the year-to-year variability of the C1 summer minima is large against a trend slope of −10.9 mm yr⁻¹. Four of the twenty observed C1 summer minima have exceeded the SD16 depth, including three of the eight most recent years (2018, 2022, 2025), while the wet years (2020, 2021, 2023, 2024) sit above SD16 by 120 to 190 mm. C2 crosses SD16 in the trend sense around 2015, with the interval extending into the pre-monitoring period; C3 lies above SD16 and its non-significant trend reaches the threshold beyond 2080; C4 sat below SD16 throughout the observed record and C5 in 18 of its 20 years.

These trends translate into progressively worsening threshold compliance. C1 has been below the wet slack summer viability threshold (−0.61 m) in all 20 monitored years, with the shallowest summer minimum recorded in 2016 (−0.647 m). C2 has similarly remained below the threshold throughout the record, with its shallowest minimum in 2005 (−0.622 m). C3 has never approached the wet slack threshold, ranging between −0.826 m and −1.458 m, and falling below the dry slack threshold (−0.98 m) in 15 of 21 years.

**Winter maximum trends **were fitted for all five clusters. C1 showed a positive but non-significant trend (+0.0075 m yr⁻¹, p = 0.184); C2 (+0.0069, p = 0.423), C3 (+0.0005, p = 0.968) and C4 (−0.0073, p = 0.700) were all non-significant. C5 showed a significant declining winter maximum trend (−0.0349 m yr⁻¹, p = 0.040): the only cluster with significant trends in both seasons.

**The C5 Coastal Forest trajectory anomaly** is the outlier. At −0.036 m yr⁻¹ in summer and −0.035 m yr⁻¹ in winter, C5\'s decline rate is 3.3 times the summer rate of C1 --- the only other cluster with a statistically significant summer trend --- and C5 is the only cluster with significant trends in both seasons. The candidate explanations are weighed in Section 5.7.2.

The post-2018 collapse in C5 seasonal amplitude (−18% raw, −21% climate-normalized; Section 4.2.1) is the largest amplitude reduction in the network: recharge peaks are no longer reaching their pre-2018 heights even after correcting for drought summers. The C5 CUSUM trajectory does not stabilize through to the end of the monitoring record.

### []{#anchor-33}**Observed Winter Maximum Flooding Record**

The observed winter flooding record shows a strong spatial contrast between structural domains (Figure 46, panel b). The C1 Lake Edge cluster exceeded the wet slack winter flooding threshold (−0.10 m) in 14 of 20 monitored years (70%). C2 Dune exceeded the threshold in 11 of 21 years (52%). C3 Western Residual exceeded the wet slack threshold in only 1 of 21 years (5%) --- occurring in 2007 --- and the dry slack threshold (−0.25 m) in 6 of 21 years. C4 Main Forest did not exceed either threshold in any monitored year. C5 Coastal Forest exceeded the wet slack threshold in 1 of 20 years (5%).

### Five-Year Mean Spring Water Level (MSL5)

The cluster-level summer-minimum trajectories examined in Sections 4.8.1--4.8.2 describe stress events --- single annual values capturing the deepest water-table excursion of each year. A vegetation community\'s response is not driven by stress events alone; it integrates the long-term baseline water level over which it grows. The 5-year mean spring water level (MSL5), as defined in Section 3.7.5 and implemented per van Willegen et al. (2025), is the metric that captures this baseline. It is the rolling 5-year mean of the cluster-mean March--May water table, taken at the end of each hydrological year. Where the summer-minimum metric is sensitive to single dry years, MSL5 is sensitive to sustained hydrological state --- the regime within which dune-slack vegetation establishes and persists.

The cluster-mean MSL5 trajectories for window-ends 2014--2025 are shown in Figure 44(a). Figure 44(b) shows, over the same window-ends, the cluster-mean four-year mean annual minimum water level, and Table 20 summarises both at window-end 2025. The two reference values drawn in Figure 44(b), from Curreli et al. (2013), are community means of the four-year (2006--09) average annual minimum water level over the 1 June--31 May hydrological year at this site --- the SD15b wet-slack community at −0.61 m and the SD16 dry-slack community at −0.98 m (their Table 4). They are therefore drawn on that quantity and counted against it; neither Curreli et al. nor van Willegen et al. (2025) define a reference value for a spring mean, and MSL5 is read without one. Until this revision the report drew the two values across MSL5, which placed every cluster about one community wetter than the reference describes.

On the quantity the reference values describe, no cluster mean reaches the SD15b community mean in any window-end from 2014 to 2025 (Table 20). C1 Lake Edge sits between −0.82 and −0.93 m, below SD15b throughout and above SD16 throughout --- the only cluster to remain above the SD16 mean. C2 Dune sits between −0.99 and −1.08 m, below the SD16 mean in every window-end but never by more than 0.10 m; C3 Western Residual (−1.16 to −1.31 m), C4 Main Forest (−1.50 to −1.95 m) and C5 Coastal Forest (−1.46 to −1.73 m) sit well below it. This agrees with the annual summer-minimum record of Section 4.8.1; both describe the trough of the year.

Two things qualify it. First, a cluster mean averages dipwells at every topographic position, dune flank included, whereas Curreli\'s means are of slack-floor quadrats, so a cluster mean sits deeper than a slack community by construction. At the eleven van Willegen piezometers with a complete 2007--10 window --- Curreli\'s own quadrats --- the per-well four-year mean annual minimum spans −0.56 to −1.38 m with a median of −0.79 m, inside the ranges her Table 4 reports for the slack communities (SD15b −0.69 to −0.51 m; SD16 −1.57 to −0.81 m). The metric reproduces at the quadrats; the depth of the cluster means is a property of how the network samples the topography. Second, the reference values are means with ranges, not viability limits, and are used here as fixed points for comparison between clusters and over time rather than as a pass--fail test.

MSL5 orders the clusters as the annual minimum does --- C1 wettest, C5 driest --- and the spread between them is of the same size on both metrics: 1.01 m between C1 and C5 on MSL5 at window-end 2025 and 0.75 m on the four-year mean annual minimum. C3 Western Residual sits 0.25 m below C2 on MSL5 at 2025 (−0.464 m against −0.216 m), and its two most recent window-ends are the two containing the wet 2023--24 hydrological year.

The forest clusters sit apart from the open dune on both metrics. On MSL5 at window-end 2025 C4 Main Forest is at −0.802 m and C5 Coastal Forest at −1.142 m, 0.67 and 1.01 m below C1; on the four-year mean annual minimum the deficits are 0.62 and 0.75 m. MSL5 is, in the van Willegen framework, primarily an open-dune metric (Section 3.5). The C5 trajectory rests on nine wells (five reference and four extended-network) located in the south-western Corsican-pine block; the cluster is the smallest in the classified network and the result should be read with that in mind, but the wells are spatially coherent and the trajectory is unambiguous within that reach.

The spatial pattern of the MSL5 surface across the network is shown in Figure 45. The figure is a piecewise-linear (Delaunay) interpolation across the 83 mapped wells --- the 85 that carry at least one valid MSL5 window, less CEH13 and CEH14, which are excluded for unreliable SSM drainage coefficients; for 75 of these the latest valid window ends in 2025, while for eight, recent gaps in spring measurements mean the latest valid window ends earlier (2015--2024), and these appear at their latest available value. The map is distinct from the cluster-mean trajectories of Figure 44 in that it shows the full spatial reach of the per-well MSL5 surface rather than the cluster-identity-based aggregation. The two figures show complementary things --- Figure 44 is cluster-mean MSL5 over time, Figure 45 is the per-well MSL5 surface at the most recent window. The map shows the deepest MSL5 concentrated in the south-western corner of the site --- the C5 Coastal Forest block --- with the surrounding open-dune network markedly shallower. The Western Residual cluster\'s western margin appears as the transition zone on the map\'s western edge, consistent with C3\'s position below C2 in the trajectory analysis.

The most recent window-ends carry a synchronous upward step. All five clusters jump wetter between window-end 2023 and window-end 2024, with the magnitude varying by cluster (Figure 44). The step reflects the 5-year window incorporating the 2023--24 hydrological year, which carried significantly higher annual rainfall than the 2018--22 range it displaces. The magnitude varies because the displacement-sensitive clusters (C4 +205 mm, C3 +157 mm, C5 +138 mm) respond more strongly than the near-surface ones (C1 +73 mm) to a single wet year entering the rolling window. Because the metric is a 5-year rolling mean, the step\'s persistence depends on subsequent years: a return to the recent dry hydrological pattern would erode it as the wet year ages out of the window. The 2025 window-end holds the step at every cluster (C5 −1.160 m at 2024, −1.142 m at 2025). The step is the entry of one wet year into the window, not a trend.

The MSL5 metric requires a five-year record of valid spring measurements. The earliest valid window-ends fall in 2010--2011 depending on cluster, but the early portion of the record carries only one to five wells contributing per cluster --- too few for cluster-mean representativeness, given within-cluster well-to-well variability of order 0.3 m at C2 and C3 and 0.4 m at C4 and C5. The trajectory plot starts at window-end 2014, which is the earliest window-end for which all five clusters carry sufficient contributing wells. Earlier window-ends are computed and stored in the supporting outputs for completeness, but are not plotted or discussed here.

The headline reading of Figure 44 is therefore threefold. MSL5 orders the clusters from the lake edge to the coastal forest and holds that order through the recorded window-ends, with the forest clusters 0.7--1.0 m below C1 at window-end 2025. On the quantity Curreli et al.\'s reference values describe, no cluster mean reaches the SD15b community mean and only C1 stays above the SD16 mean --- a statement about cluster means over a network that samples every topographic position, while the calibrated slack-floor piezometers themselves sit inside the published ranges. The 2024 step is climatic and is held at 2025. Implications for the climate trajectory are taken up in Section 4.13.1; the relation between this reading and the summer-minimum reading of Section 4.8.1 is returned to in Section 5.1.

### Equilibrium Wetness Index and Vegetation Cross-Validation

MSL5 (Section 4.8.3; defined Section 3.7.5) follows van Willegen et al. (2025), who identified it as the strongest single hydrological correlate of dune-slack vegetation moisture at Newborough. Reconstructing per-well MSL5 for the seventeen van Willegen piezometers reproduces their published mean spring levels to within approximately 11 mm once the fixed dipwell-versus-quadrat datum offset is removed, and between wells MSL5 predicts mean Ellenberg-F --- the moisture indicator value (wetness scale 1--12; Hill et al., 1999) --- strongly (r = +0.83, n = 18). The validated wells lie in the lake-edge, open-dune and western-residual clusters, van Willegen having placed no quadrats in the forest interior.

The state-space coefficients afford a structurally-derived estimate of the same wetness. Setting the mean monthly change to zero in the fitted model (Section 3.4) and inverting the head-dependent drainage term yields an equilibrium water-table level, h_eq = (β₁P̄ − β₂PET̄)/β₃ − z₀ (z₀ = 3.7 m), from each well\'s coefficients and the long-term annual-mean climate. Tested directly against Ellenberg-F this equilibrium index performs as well as observed MSL5: the two are statistically indistinguishable as vegetation predictors (Figure 48; Table 21), their correlation confidence intervals overlapping almost entirely and a Williams test for the difference between the two dependent correlations returning p = 0.45. The equivalence holds not only in aggregate but well by well: binned by prediction accuracy, the two metrics are broadly comparable across match bands, the equilibrium index placing marginally more wells in the closest band but also more in the poorest (Table 22). That coefficients calibrated purely on month-to-month dynamics predict vegetation moisture as well as the direct spring-level metric is the result; eighteen wells give limited statistical power, so this is equivalence within the data rather than proven identity. Because the equilibrium index is computed from the coefficients and climate alone, this comparison is independent of MSL5 --- each metric is regressed on Ellenberg-F separately, so the equivalence tests two independent predictors rather than restating the spring-level metric. No single state-space coefficient predicts Ellenberg-F nearly as well (best \|r\| ≈ 0.5, versus 0.79 for the equilibrium index), the vegetation signal residing in the equilibrium level rather than any individual rate or storage term.

Beyond predicting vegetation, the equilibrium index can be calibrated onto the MSL5 scale itself by ordinary least squares. Consistent with MSL5\'s own open-dune character (Section 4.8.3) and with the forest coefficients being the least constrained on the site (Section 4.9.2), this calibration is scoped to the open-dune network (clusters C1--C3, reference and extended wells): MSL5 = 0.257 + 0.959·EWI (n = 62, r = 0.98, RMSE = 61 mm). Every open-dune well is reconstructed within 150 mm, and the relationship generalizes beyond the vegetation-calibrated subset, with a root-mean-square error of 60 mm across the 46 open-dune wells outside van Willegen\'s seventeen-piezometer set against 63 mm on the calibration wells. The C4/C5 forest wells are predicted but held out of scope (n = 20, RMSE 152 mm): there the coefficients are least constrained and the estimate is too coarse to place a well across a Curreli threshold. The full per-well reconstruction, with the out-of-scope forest wells flagged, is given in Table S7.1 of the Supplementary Material.

**Precision of the two indices**

The two indices differ in what limits them. MSL5 averages five spring observations, so its precision is set by how far spring levels swing from year to year: the interannual standard deviation rises from about 175 mm at C1 through 251 mm at C2 and 315 mm at C3 to 277 mm at C5 and 404 mm at C4, giving a five-year window mean a standard error of about 78, 112, 141, 124 and 181 mm respectively. The equilibrium index carries no window, but it divides by β₃, so its precision is set by how well that coefficient is identified. Propagating each well\'s β₃ uncertainty gives a standard error of about 316 mm at C1, 454 mm at C2, 512 mm at C3, 430 mm at C5 and 1112 mm at C4.

The equilibrium index is therefore the less precise of the two throughout the network, by a factor of between 3.5 and 6.0 at the cluster medians, and it is more precise than a five-year MSL5 mean at none of the 65 wells where both can be computed. Its advantages lie elsewhere: it requires no five-year spring window, so it can be computed at wells whose spring record is too broken for MSL5, and its precision shows no measurable dependence on record length (β₃ relative standard error against number of observations, Spearman −0.17, p = 0.48 across the extended network). The two indices also degrade at the same wells for opposite reasons --- MSL5 where spring levels swing furthest, the equilibrium index where β₃ is weakly identified --- and the forest clusters are adverse on both counts at once. Under closed canopy both carry a precision caveat, and the Ellenberg-F equivalence established above rests on eighteen open-dune piezometers, van Willegen having placed no quadrats in the forest interior.

### Slack-floor wet area: an independent spatial check on the modelled water table

The vegetation cross-validation of Section 4.8.4 tests the modelled water table against an independent ecological record at the wells and quadrats; it does not test whether the modelled level predicts the wetted extent of the slack floor between them. A wholly independent check on that spatial reach is available from the Sentinel-2 satellite archive (Script 45), which images the warren every few days at 10 m resolution in the near-infrared, where standing water and saturated ground read dark. Over 43 cloud-free winter scenes (2016--2026) the open dune-slack floor of the warren --- a 306.97 ha study area of 30,697 cells, the planted forest excluded --- was classified into two near-infrared wetness classes: open water (the darkest cells) and wet floor (dark but not ponded). This is an area measure derived entirely from satellite reflectance; it shares no wells, no data and no model coefficients with the SSM water table.

Across the 43 scenes each class area rises with the contemporaneous median water level as area = a·exp(b·h), where h is the reference-network median level relative to the slack floor. Open water grows steeply (a = 24.9 ha, b = 4.43; Spearman ρ = +0.80, R² = 0.71) and wet floor more gradually (a = 56.1 ha, b = 0.95; ρ = +0.85, R² = 0.77) over the observed level range −0.80 to +0.03 m (Figure 49). At its most extensive the darkened floor (wet floor plus open water) has reached 11,703 cells (117.0 ha), of which up to 4,483 (44.8 ha) have been open water. The fits establish that satellite-observed slack wetness is a monotonic, well-behaved function of the modelled level --- the precondition for using it as a spatial test.

That test is whether the modelled water table, driven through these fitted curves, reproduces the observed wet-area history it never saw. Passing the SSM monthly level (Section 4.4) through the two curves yields a modelled open-water and wet-floor area for every month of record; comparing these to the satellite-observed areas over the months with adequate well coverage (n = 238 well-months, ≥ 20 reporting wells) tests the model out of sample and in space (Figure 50). Wet-floor area is reproduced closely (R² = 0.78 under the recharge-referenced level, 0.80 under the calibrated level; median modelled:observed area ratio 0.96 in both modes), open water more approximately (R² = 0.62 and 0.64; median ratio 0.84 and 0.81, the model running slightly dry at the ponded extreme).

This is the report\'s only spatial, out-of-sample validation of the modelled water table. The well hydrographs (Section 3.4.2) validate it through time at points, and the vegetation record (Section 4.8.4) validates it against ecology at points; neither tests whether the modelled level predicts the wetted extent of the slack floor between the wells. The satellite-observed extent is recovered from the model, most strongly for the wet-floor class that carries the dune-slack habitat signal (Section 5.7.6). The check is an aggregate one over the whole warren floor, not a per-slack map (the per-slack aerial comparison was withdrawn as unresolvable, D-168), and it is confined to the open warren; the planted forest is not modelled and is excluded. The wet-area model is presented as an illustration of the area--level relationship, not as a flood map (D-177). Its implications for the dune-slack habitat area at stake under the climate trajectory are taken up in Section 5.

The same scene stack, read cell by cell, gives the wetted extent a spatial expression the aggregate curves cannot (Figure 51). For each 10 m cell of the slack floor the scenes are ordered by the reference-network median level at their dates, and the cell\'s switching level is the level at which it first reads wet floor, and separately open water: a ground-referenced height of the water table at that cell, resolved at 10 m and independent of the wells. Of the 30,697 floor cells 11,703 have read wet floor and 4,483 open water within the observed range of −0.80 to +0.03 m; the remainder have not wetted in the record. The maps are the floor\'s own answer to where the water table reaches the ground first, and they carry two cautions. They are not the prediction of a digital elevation model plus a uniformly rising water table --- that construction, from the 50 m head surface of Section 4.9.5 and the 10 m floor, has no skill at cell scale, because the interpolated surface cannot resolve slack-scale relief (Figure 57). And the floor lags the wells on the way down: at the same median level a scene taken while the water table is rising carries 2.2 times the open water of one taken while it is falling (wet floor 1.15 times; the phase term is significant at p = 0.003 and 0.04). Rainfall in the scene month adds no positive term once the level is in the model. The aggregate fits of Figure 49 are level-only by design (D-178) and absorb this hysteresis into their scatter (Script 45: 45_03_switching_levels_map.png, 45_04_phase_hysteresis.csv).

## []{#anchor-34}**Spatial Groundwater Analysis**

The per-well SSM reparametrization provides a spatially resolved view of aquifer behaviour that complements the cluster-level summaries of Sections 4.2--4.4. This section presents the spatial coefficient structure across the 88 well classified network (66 reference wells with per-well SSM coefficients; 22 extended wells assigned cluster-level coefficients via the Pearson affinity audit of Section 3.3), the baseline head surface and groundwater flow field, and the SSM water balance residual; the equilibrium scenario projections under prescribed climate and forest management perturbations that these fields feed are presented in Section 4.13. An interactive scenario viewer (Hollingham, 2026) integrates these outputs with the Curreli et al. (2013) ecological thresholds and is available as a companion tool to this report.

### []{#anchor-35}Datum Sensitivity 

Per-well drainage datum optimization (Figure 52a), obtained by independently optimizing the displacement datum z₀ at each well to maximize SSM fit (Section 3.4), shows that the R²-maximizing datum varies systematically across the site: the cluster medians are 0.7 m at C1 Lake Edge, 0.9 m at C2 Dune, 1.6 m at C3 Western Residual, 1.9 m at C5 Coastal Forest and 2.8 m at C4 Main Forest (network median 1.35 m), and the per-well value correlates with mean depth to water (r = 0.59, n = 66). The R² gain from per-well optimization over the uniform 3.7 m datum has a median of 0.017 and exceeds 0.05 at nine wells, reaching 0.093 at C1 and 0.070 at the eastern C2 wells where the effective drainage base is shallowest (Figure 52b); it is below 0.01 at every forest well. The uniform datum is not the fit-optimal choice at the shallow-water-table wells; Section 3.4.1 states its cost and why it is retained.

Per-well SSM coefficients interpolated across the site (Section 3.4.3) reveal spatially variable patterns whose broad structure aligns with the cluster boundaries (Figure 53a--d), although within-cluster heterogeneity is substantial. All coefficient surfaces are interpolated by piecewise-linear (Delaunay) interpolation to a 50 m grid with dune ridge cells masked where the DEM raster exceeds the interpolated surface by more than 1 m (see Section 3.8).

### []{#anchor-36}Spatial Coefficient Structure

The R² surface (Figure 53a), derived from per-well SSM fits at each well\'s optimal drainage datum, shows the model explains 70--85% of monthly water table variance across the central and northern open dune, declining toward the forest (C4 and C5 mean 0.68) and some peripheral south-eastern wells. Since the R² gain from per-well datum optimization is small outside the lake-edge and eastern dune wells (Figure 52b), these values are close to the effective fit quality under the standard pipeline datum, and above it at C1.

The three coefficient surfaces (Figure 53b--d) reveal a coherent spatial story about how rainfall enters, is consumed, and drains from the aquifer. Recharge sensitivity (β₁) is highest in the north-east around the C1 Lake Edge wells closest to Llyn Rhos-Ddu (\>5 mm/mm), declines across the open dune (3--5 mm/mm), and drops to 2--3 mm/mm west of the forest boundary. Atmospheric draw (β₂) shows a different geography: the highest values occur in two zones --- the C4 Main Forest interior and a band across the northern open dune adjacent to the ridge --- while C1 Lake Edge wells show notably low values (mean 0.54 mm/mm). C5 Coastal Forest shows moderate β₂ (mean 1.13), lower than C4 despite also carrying pine canopy. Drainage rate (β₃, logarithmic scale) shows the strongest spatial contrast of any coefficient: C1 and northern C2 wells drain fastest (\>8% of displacement per month), the forest interior shows the lowest rates in the network (C4 mean 1.6%, with individual wells below 1%), and C5 falls between the two (mean 4.6%). One C4 well (CEH14) records a negative β₃ (−2.1%), although the estimate is not significantly different from zero (p = 0.14), and six of the nine C4 wells likewise carry a non-significant β₃ on the 100-month per-well window from which these surfaces are built. That weakness is largely a property of the window rather than of the cluster: refitting each well on its full record leaves seven of the nine significant, with only CEH13 and CEH14 failing. The mapped C4 coefficients are therefore best read as the least precisely resolved in the network, rather than as evidence that forest-interior drainage is unresolvable.

Within the C3 Western Residual cluster, the coefficient surfaces resolve into a coherent internal gradient aligned with the south-west to north-east axis --- the same axis as distance inland from the eroding south-west coast. Projecting the 21 C3 well positions onto this axis, recharge sensitivity β₁ increases inland (r = +0.76, p \< 0.001), drainage rate β₃ increases inland (r = +0.58, p = 0.009), and WTF-derived specific yield declines inland, from approximately 0.41 at the south-west margin to 0.25 at the north-east (r = −0.83, p \< 0.001). The interpretation of this gradient is developed in Section 5.6.1.

The combined picture is of an aquifer whose eastern margin fills quickly, loses water quickly, and resets each season, while its western and forested interior fills slowly, holds water against evaporative demand, and drains sluggishly --- the \"shallow pan\" versus \"deep sponge\" contrast identified at cluster level in Section 4.2.

### []{#anchor-37}**Drainage Decay Half-Life**

The drainage decay half-life t½ = ln(2)/β₃ (Figure 54; Section 3.4.5) maps the time for excess groundwater storage above the drainage datum to drain to half its initial value at each reference well. It is derived from the SSM drainage coefficient β₃ alone, without requiring an independent storage estimate. The eastern open dune shows the shortest half-lives in the network: C1 Lake Edge t½ = 5.9--8.9 months (mean 7.8 months), meaning excess storage is largely dissipated within a single season; C2 Dune t½ = 6.3--13.1 months (mean 10.3 months). The western dune shows intermediate values: C3 Western Residual t½ = 6.8--19.9 months (mean 13.2 months). The forest clusters show markedly longer half-lives: C5 Coastal Forest t½ = 11.4--15.8 months (mean 14.0 months), comparable to C3 despite carrying pine canopy (Section 4.9.4); and C4 Main Forest t½ = 16.2--43.1 months (mean 26.0 months), the longest half-lives in the network. At the upper end of the C4 range, excess groundwater storage persists for some three and a half years before draining to half its initial level. The per-well values are on each well\'s full record (D-192; Section 3.4.5): on the 100-month comparison window the C4 recessions are comparable with the window itself and are not identified there (Section 3.4), so the window values overstate them --- 17--82 months, mean 38, at C4. The pronounced C4 hotspot lies on the elevated plateau, where β₃ is lowest (Section 5.2.3). The wide within-C4 range (16--43 months on the full record) shows the forest block to be hydraulically non-uniform. CEH14 (negative β₃) and CEH13 (near-zero β₃) are excluded as ridge-flank wells where β₃ is not reliably identified; t½ = ln(2)/β₃ cannot meaningfully be formed from a negative or near-zero coefficient.

The model benchmarking diagnostic (Section 4.4; Figure 17) complements the half-life map. The iterative NSE improvement from SSM over TLM (ΔNSE) correlates positively with β₃ (r = 0.60, p \< 0.001) and negatively with β₂ (r = -0.62, p \< 0.001). The TLM fails most severely at C1 Lake Edge (median ΔNSE = +1.52, median TLM NSE = -0.90), where β₃ is highest, and least severely at C4 Main Forest (median ΔNSE = +0.41, median TLM NSE = +0.25), where β₃ is lowest (Section 5.2.4).

**When t½ and ΔNSE are plotted together with point size scaled by Sy (Figure 55), the five cluster centroids occupy distinct regions of the diagnostic space, though the separation is moderate and individual wells overlap appreciably within it. C1 Lake Edge sits at short t½, high ΔNSE and low Sy; C4 Main Forest at long t½, low ΔNSE and intermediate Sy; C5 Coastal Forest is displaced from C4 in t½ and storage despite sharing the same pine canopy, at intermediate t½ and higher Sy, with the higher ΔNSE; C2 and C3 span the middle ground, C3 at the longer t½ and higher Sy. This diagnostic space is derived independently of the Ward\'s clustering applied to the raw hydrograph data; its reading as aquifer architecture is in Section 5.1.**

### []{#anchor-38} Per-Well Forest Zone Analysis

The spatial coefficient atlas (Figure 53b--d) shows that the C4 and C5 forest wells span nearly the full site-wide range of β₂ values despite sharing the same Corsican pine canopy. To test whether this within-forest variation tracks topographic position (a proxy for the uncored substrate) or canopy differences, per-well SSM coefficients for the 14 forest zone wells (9 in C4, 5 in C5) were regressed against elevation, distance from the ridge and Easting (Section 3.4.4).

Elevation is overwhelmingly the dominant spatial predictor (Table 23). The atmospheric draw coefficient β₂ shows the strongest relationship (r = 0.983, p \< 0.001; R² = 0.967; leave-one-out predicted R² = 0.955, the out-of-sample check for n = 14), with higher-elevation wells on the ridge returning systematically higher β₂ values. Adding distance from the ridge contributes virtually no additional explanatory power (R² = 0.967). The drainage coefficient β₃ shows a significant but weaker elevation dependence (r = −0.831, p \< 0.001; R² = 0.691), with distance from the ridge adding meaningful information (combined R² = 0.788): wells further from the ridge and at lower elevation drain faster. The recharge coefficient β₁ shows no significant relationship with elevation (r = 0.192, p = 0.512); Easting is the best single predictor (r = 0.579, p = 0.030) but explains only 34% of variance. This elevation--drainage relationship is visible directly in the drainage decay half-life map (Figure 54), where C4 wells reach t½ values of up to 82 months compared with 12--18 months at C5.

C4 and C5 form two clearly distinct groups rather than a continuum. They separate almost entirely on the β₂ axis: C4 wells cluster at β₂ = 2.0--3.8 while C5 wells sit at β₂ = 0.8--1.4, with zero overlap. Mean elevations differ significantly (C4: 10.6 m, C5: 5.6 m; p \< 0.001), with a clean gap between 6.4 m and 8.6 m containing no wells (Source: 10c_forest_zone_cluster_summary.csv). This corresponds to the transition from the elevated ridge and plateau terrain to the low-lying coastal fringe. Both zones carry Corsican pine canopy; C4 sits on the flank of the bedrock ridge (which outcrops within the forest), C5 on the lower coastal sand (Section 5.6.1).

Two individual wells merit comment. CEH14, at the highest elevation in the forest zone (14.4 m), has the highest β₂ in the network (3.828), on the elevation regression line. Its negative β₃ (****−0.021****) and low R² (0.586) are not well identified at this ridge-proximal position. The estimate is not significantly different from zero (p = 0.14), and ****six**** of the nine C4 wells likewise carry a non-significant β₃ (Section 5.2.3). NW10, the broadleaf block well, has the highest β₁ in the forest zone (****3.4****81****, ****2.4 SD**** above the C4 mean) and the highest β₃ among C4 wells (****0.040****). Its reading is in Section 5.6.3.

**The per-well analysis places the C4/C5 partition of the Ward\'s solution at an elevation discontinuity; its mechanistic interpretation --- and its implications for forest management --- is developed in Section 5.6.1.**

### Mean Water Table Surface and Groundwater Flow Direction

The mean annual water table surface was constructed by piecewise-linear (Delaunay) interpolation of per-well mean maOD values (2005--2026) to a 50 m grid on the British National Grid, masked to the rectangular sea-boundary extent (Figure 56; Section 3.8.1). No DEM-height mask is applied: the water table is a continuous surface that need not sit below the ground everywhere, and in the slacks it periodically does not. The highest mean water levels (\~14 m AOD) occur in the north-western forest zone adjacent to the bedrock ridge, declining to 7--9 m AOD across the central dune and reaching 2--3 m AOD at the southern and eastern coastal margins. Contours run approximately NE--SW across the site. Groundwater flow direction vectors, the unit-normalised negative head gradient (direction only; no hydraulic conductivity or aquifer thickness enters the construction), show a radial pattern diverging from the north-western high point: predominantly southward and south-westward in the western half of the site, and south-eastward in the eastern half. The blue lines in Figure 56 are the surface flow routing derived from the LiDAR DTM (Conrad et al., 2015; Natural Resources Wales LiDAR DTM, 2023): they mark where water would collect on the ground surface --- the slack floors --- and are drawn as topographic context, not as evidence of groundwater flow direction: the slack floors they trace are deflation surfaces cut to the water table of the time (Ranwell, 1959), so the routing and the head field are not independent, and their agreement is expected rather than a test. The flow vectors are reported as directional context for the interpolated head field rather than as output of a calibrated continuous-flow model.

The highest water levels (\~14 m AOD) occur in the north-western forest zone adjacent to the bedrock ridge, declining toward the southern and eastern coastal margins (\~2--3 m AOD). Groundwater flow direction vectors (white arrows) are the unit-normalised negative head gradient: direction only, magnitude not scaled, and no hydraulic conductivity or aquifer thickness enters them. Blue lines: surface flow routing from the LiDAR DTM, shown as topographic context --- it traces the slack floors, which are themselves cut to the water table, so it is not independent evidence of groundwater flow direction. Well symbols are coloured by cluster. Background: LiDAR greyscale hillshade (LiDAR data: © NRW & OS; see Section 10 for full attribution). Generated by 20_spatial_figures.py. (Source: 20_head_surface_streams.png)

How closely the water table follows the ground, and at what scale, is measured directly (Figure 57). Regressed on the DEM at native resolution over the 1,269 grid cells inside the reference-network hull, the head surface has slope 0.65 and r = 0.75; smoothed to 300 m the ground gives slope 0.99 and r = 0.92, and the relation does not tighten further beyond that. The water table is therefore a subdued replica of the topography: it follows the dune mound from the bedrock ridge to the coast almost 1:1 and does not follow the ridge-and-slack relief beneath \~300 m. That threshold is also close to the finest relief the network can resolve --- the median nearest-well spacing is 123 m --- so the measurement bounds the scale from above rather than fixing it. At the 66 reference wells themselves the mean water table tracks the surveyed ground at slope 0.98 (r = 0.99), which is a different relation: dipwells stand on slack floors, and slack floors are deflation surfaces cut down to the water table (Ranwell, 1959), so at the wells the ground follows the water table rather than the reverse.

### []{#anchor-39}Water Balance Residual Field

The SSM water balance residual field (Figure 58; Section 3.8.1) quantifies the degree to which the three-term SSM closes the long-term water balance at each well. The residual at each reference well is computed as α_B = (β₂·PET̄ + β₃·h̄\_disp) − β₁·P̄, where overbars denote long-term monthly means, h̄\_disp is mean displacement above the 3.7 m drainage datum, and P̄ is gross rainfall. The averaging window is taken from the mean-head record itself (March 2005 to February 2026, n = 252 months; P̄ = 74.11 mm/month, PET̄ = 54.39 mm/month), so that the climate means and the mean heads describe the same period.

Gross rather than interception-corrected rainfall is used at forest wells. Script 03 fits the SSM on gross rainfall and above-canopy Thornthwaite PET, so the canopy interception loss is already carried inside the fitted β₂·PET̄ term; reducing P̄ as well would subtract it twice. Interception is a partition of the atmospheric energy budget rather than a term additive to it (Section 3.8).

Positive values indicate locations where modelled losses exceed modelled recharge, implying an unmodelled input; negative values indicate the converse. The field closes tightly and carries no coherent spatial structure, with a small systematic negative offset. Residuals span −0.0133 to +0.0044 m/month about a median of −0.0046 m/month (mean −0.0038), with 64 of the 66 reference wells falling within ±0.01 m/month and 54 negative. All five cluster medians are negative, ranging from −0.0074 m/month at C4 Main Forest to −0.0001 m/month at C1 Lake Edge, all small relative to the coefficient uncertainties that generate them. No DEM-height mask is applied. Residual magnitude is uncorrelated with position on either axis (Spearman ρ = −0.055 against Easting, p = 0.66; ρ = +0.093 against Northing, p = 0.46). The signed residual shows no gradient on either axis (ρ = −0.024 against Easting, p = 0.85; ρ = −0.116 against Northing, p = 0.35).

No well exceeds +0.02 m/month, and only twelve of the sixty-six carry a positive residual at all. The largest positive values are CEH4 (+0.0044) in C3 Western Residual, CEH23 (+0.0025) in C1 Lake Edge and CEH17 (+0.0024) in C5 Coastal Forest, with CEH18 (+0.0019) in C3 and NW9 (+0.0019) in C5 next --- all in the open dune, at the lake edge or at the coastal forest margin rather than at the ridge. No C4 Main Forest well is positive. The largest negative residual occurs at the open-dune well D7 (−0.0133 m/month), with the ridge-flank well CEH14 (−0.0110 m/month) close behind; at both, modelled recharge marginally exceeds modelled losses.

The residual field is read in Section 5.2.1. Across all five clusters the three-term SSM closes the long-term water balance without requiring an additional input term, and the corrected field agrees with the independent water balance of Script 16, which computes the same closure on gross rainfall over the study period and agrees to within ±5.8 mm/month at every cluster, the largest discrepancy falling at C4 Main Forest. The independently computed Darcy flow vectors derived from the mean head gradient field indicate a radial flux diverging from the north-western high point --- southward and south-westward in the western half of the site, south-eastward in the eastern half (Section 4.9.5); they are retained as directional context for the site\'s flow geometry and are not evidence bearing on the residual field, which shows no ridge-proximal signal.

## **Coastal erosion and the cross-shore section**

The spatial analysis of Section 4.9 asks how quantities vary in plan view, over easting and northing, and answers by interpolation. This section asks a different question of the same network: how does change vary along a single coordinate, the perpendicular distance to the eroding shoreline, and it answers by fitting a physical decay law. Same wells, same records, different geometry. The change of coordinate is what makes a far field definable at all, and with it the identification problem set out below. This is the boundary-referenced view of the network, not a transect cut through the maps of Section 4.9.

### **The cross-shore coordinate and what it replaces**

Every quantity in this section is indexed by d, the perpendicular distance from a well to the eroding Caernarfon Bay high-water mark. The coordinate is computed within the pipeline from a committed OpenStreetMap mean-high-water polyline (EPSG:27700), restricted to the west-facing Newborough frontage; the Menai Strait and Llanddwyn Island are excluded as non-eroding boundaries, so a well\'s distance is to the shoreline that is actually retreating and not to the nearest water.

That restriction is the substantive part of the definition. An unrestricted distance-to-water would place the eastern lake-edge wells within a few hundred metres of a boundary, and the gradient fitted here would be a fit to the wrong coastline.

The coordinate replaces easting as the spatial variable for questions about coastal forcing. Easting serves that role in the BACI design of Section 4.6, where it absorbs west-to-east divergence between treatment and control wells, and its coefficient is not a measurement of coastal retreat (Section 4.6.3). The reason is visible once the coordinate is stated: easting is a proxy for distance to the shore only to the extent that the shoreline runs north--south, and within the fifteen wells of the clearfell panel that correspondence fails entirely. Distance to the eroding boundary is the variable the physics is written in; easting is a nuisance covariate that happens to correlate with it across the network and not within a compartment of it.

### **Network-scale partition of the summer-minimum decline.** 

The third candidate mechanism for the C5 anomaly --- progressive coastal boundary retreat --- can be tested quantitatively at network scale. A non-linear panel regression was fitted to the full 21-year monthly record (12,006 observations across 67 wells; FE wells, the scraped well CEH36, the BACI clearfell-zone wells and the bedrock-ridge well CEH12 excluded) to test whether the C5 anomaly is quantitatively consistent with coastal boundary retreat operating site-wide. Each well\'s perpendicular distance to the eroding Caernarfon Bay High Water Mark was computed within the pipeline from a committed OpenStreetMap mean-high-water coastline (Menai Strait and Llanddwyn Island excluded as non-eroding boundaries). The headline fit is the forest-free panel (the wells under canopy on the land-cover flag dropped; 61 wells, 10,929 observations), giving a Dupuit--Forchheimer steady-state strip-aquifer form. The headline coast-edge trend is quoted at the 150 m reference distance, which sits inside the observed range of well positions: −26.2 ± 3.6 mm yr⁻¹ (95 % CI −33.2 to −19.2, well basis). The fitted decay amplitude at the shoreline, δ₀ = −31.3 ± 4.9 mm yr⁻¹, is reported as a model parameter and not as the headline: no well sits at the shoreline, so d = 0 lies beyond the network and is the one distance at which the linear-capped and exponential forms disagree materially --- a spread of 9.3 mm yr⁻¹ there against 1.6 mm yr⁻¹ at 150 m. The amplitude carries one well\'s leverage: withholding ceh3, the second-nearest well to the shore at 176 m, moves δ₀ by 3.2 mm yr⁻¹ and the 150 m rate by 2.4 mm yr⁻¹, 1.9 times the next-largest single-well shift (each well withheld in turn over the 61-well panel; 25_16_delta0_leave_one_out.csv). Uncertainties on the coastal gradient are quoted on the well basis: the standard error is estimated from those refits, because consecutive monthly readings within a well are not independent observations, and the fitted standard errors from the monthly rows remain in 25_01_panel_fit_parameters.csv as the nominal precision of the model and are not quoted as uncertainties (D-147). On that basis δ₀ is −31.3 ± 4.9 mm yr⁻¹, more than six standard errors from zero, and the leverage of ceh3 lies inside the error --- a property of a network with few wells inside 300 m rather than an instability of the fit. The fit gives an inland reach L_cg of about 900 m (± 128 m, well basis) beyond which the gradient effect vanishes, and a far-field asymptote c_far of −0.1 ± 0.6 mm yr⁻¹, which is not a climate rate and is not quoted as one (Section 4.10.3). Model selection by AIC favours the exponential form (ΔAIC = −4.9); the linear-with-cutoff form is retained on physical grounds, as the Dupuit--Forchheimer steady-state solution for a strip aquifer with a fixed inland reach, and because the exponential's far-field asymptote takes the opposite sign to the observed far-field trend --- not on the AIC margin, which points the other way. The fit is robust to forest-cover exclusion: it is itself the forest-free panel, and the full-network and C3-only fits shift no parameter beyond sampling uncertainty (Script 25; Figure 59).

Applied to C5\'s mean coast-proximity, the model predicts a gradient contribution of −18.3 mm yr⁻¹. The decomposition is computed against a balanced observed basis --- the slope of the annual cross-well mean of the per-well summer minima, −16.1 mm yr⁻¹ --- rather than against the cluster-centroid slope of −35.9 mm yr⁻¹, because a mean taken over per-well fits reports the composition of record lengths as though it were a rate: within C5 the two wells with twenty years of record average −32.4 mm yr⁻¹ while the single ten-year record returns −59.2. On that basis the gradient accounts for C5\'s decline within uncertainty, leaving −0.7 mm yr⁻¹ unexplained. The panel\'s climate term is +2.9 mm yr⁻¹, acting against the decline rather than adding to it, and the far-field offset is −0.1 mm yr⁻¹; the two are not separately identified and only their sum, +2.8 mm yr⁻¹, is recovered. ****This attribution should be read against the sampling base of the forest-free fit. The forest-free panel that anchors δ₀ and L_cg excludes most C4 and C5 wells, and three of the five C5 wells meet the per-well summer-min slope criterion that feeds the cluster-mean perpendicular distance to coast. The cluster centroid slope itself is computed over all five C5 wells, so the direction of the C5 result is robust --- C5 is unambiguously the most coastal-affected cluster --- but the precise magnitude remains sensitive to which C5 wells enter the forest-free filter.**** C1 and C2 lie beyond the fitted inland reach L_cg and carry no coastal term at all, and C3 and C4 sit just inside it, so at four of the five clusters most of the observed decline is left unexplained by the model --- and what is left is the same at each. Taking the balanced observed decline less the modelled coastal gradient, the three open-dune clusters agree at −11.0 mm yr⁻¹ with a spread of 0.18 mm yr⁻¹, across seven, twenty-eight and seventeen wells on different substrates and at different distances from the sea. The independent site-mean trend of Section 5.7.5 gives −13.1 mm yr⁻¹ over the same record. The agreement establishes that this residual decline is spatially uniform; it does not resolve its rate, because the clusters share the same year-to-year weather and their errors are therefore common-mode rather than independent, leaving −11.0 inside the ±28.8 mm yr⁻¹ minimum detectable rate. It is reported as an unexplained uniform loss rather than as a climate rate (Section 5.7.5). ****The per-cluster decomposition is tabulated in Table 24 (and visualized in Figure 59) and itemises each cluster\'s observed centroid slope partitioned into the climate-uniform background, the coastal-retreat gradient contribution evaluated at the cluster\'s mean coast-proximity, and the unattributed residual.**** The weighing of this result against the other candidate mechanisms for the C5 anomaly is in Section 5.7.2.

### **What the fit cannot resolve: the far-field level**

The decay model carries a third parameter, the constant c_far, to which the profile decays inland. On the committed fit it is −0.10 mm yr⁻¹ (SE 0.55) --- small, and indistinguishable from zero. That value should not be read as a measurement of the site-wide background rate, and the reason is worth setting out, because it is the same limitation Section 5.7.5 reaches from a different direction.

The constant is separately identified but not stably estimated. Within any one fitting window it is cleanly separable from the cumulative-water-balance covariate the panel uses to absorb spatially uniform climate forcing: its variance inflation factor against that covariate is 1.01 after within-well and month demeaning. Before those fixed effects are removed the same two covariates are very nearly collinear (variance inflation about 151), because a cumulative sum of a near-constant-mean series is almost a straight line in time; the small figure is a property of the demeaned design and should not be quoted without it. What moves the constant is the choice of window. Holding the well set fixed and advancing only the first month of the fit, the constant runs from −0.10 to +24.20 mm yr⁻¹ while the coast-edge amplitude stays negative throughout and the reach barely moves. The instability is not sampling error: across fixed-length rolling windows the constant moves seven to sixteen times its own within-window standard error.

The constant and the climate covariate compensate. Sliding a window of constant length along the record, the constant and the covariate\'s trend contribution correlate at −0.60 to −0.82 depending on window length: when the covariate is apportioned more of the decline, the constant takes less, and the reverse. Their sum is better determined than either part, and the spread of both narrows sharply as the window lengthens (Figure 60) --- at eighteen years the constant settles to −0.20 mm yr⁻¹ with a standard deviation of 4.64, against 13.16 at ten years.

No far-field rate is therefore quoted anywhere in this work, and the site-wide component of the decline is treated under the recharge-efficiency and seasonal-redistribution account of Section 5 rather than here.

Over the well record potential evapotranspiration at RAF Valley rises by 1.96 mm yr⁻¹ (t = 2.67). That short-window figure should be read against the long record rather than as a secular rate: PET rises by 0.32 mm yr⁻¹ over 1931--2025 (t = 4.51) and by 0.59 over 1960--2025 (t = 5.03), so the trend is real, of long standing, and steepening. It is also the only climate term at this site that separates from zero, and the reason is variability rather than magnitude --- PET varies by about 3% about its mean where winter rainfall varies by about 19%, so PET\'s rise over the well record is close to two standard deviations of its own year-to-year scatter while winter rainfall\'s is under one. The winter trend is the larger of the two in millimetres and the smaller relative to its own noise.

What does not change is the balance. The summer (June--September) water balance trends at −4.19 mm yr⁻¹ and the winter (October--March) balance at +3.74 mm yr⁻¹. Neither is individually distinguishable from zero (t = −1.28 and +0.84), and neither is claimed to be; what matters is that they are of opposite sign and comparable size, so that their sum --- which is what an annual term sees --- is +1.10 mm yr⁻¹ with t = 0.27, which is flat. The far-field constant is fitted against a covariate built from that annual balance (Section 5.7.7).

The rolling-window output should not be read as a climate history. A ten-year water-balance trend at this site is dominated by which extreme years fall inside the window, and the constant inherits that window sensitivity, which is why it is not quoted and why it settles only at window lengths long enough that no single year can dominate.

### **Independent transect estimate of the coastal drawdown rate**

The δ₀ of the panel regression above is cross-checked directly, and without a model, along a single coast-to-inland transect. Taking MAM spring means from the most coastal well (CEH22, at the dune toe) and an inland anchor beyond the fitted reach L_cg (NW4, ≈1 km inland), the coast-minus-inland head difference deepens progressively across 2010--2023 at −27.8 mm yr⁻¹ (95 % CI −36.1 to −19.3; n = 14; AR(1)-corrected; Figure 61) --- within error of the network-scale δ₀ of −31.3 mm yr⁻¹, from an entirely independent construction, and robust to any single year (leave-one-out slopes −32.2 to −25.5 mm yr⁻¹). The divergence is shared between its two ends: CEH22 falls at −14.6 mm yr⁻¹ in absolute terms while the inland anchor rises at +13.2 mm yr⁻¹ over the same springs, so the growing gradient combines the interior refilling through the wet springs of the window with the coast dropping. The observed offset grows monotonically (anchor-referenced coastal-end ordering Spearman ρ = −0.79, against −0.21 for the raw levels), and spring climate water balance does not trend over the window; what the growing offset distinguishes is set out in Section 5.7.3. The estimate remains a single line of four wells over a window opening after drawdown was already underway, so it distinguishes a growing (erosion-like) gradient from a static one rather than resolving erosion from a time-varying substrate effect (Section 5.7.3).

The difference deepens at −27.8 mm yr⁻¹ (95% CI −36.1 to −19.3; n = 14), within error of the network-scale δ₀ of −31.3 mm yr⁻¹ from the independent gradient regression (grey annotation). ### Coastal-Margin Processes and the Easting Gradient

The forest drawdown propagation map (Figure 65) raises a natural comparison: how does the spatial reach of canopy-driven drawdown compare with the coastal-margin processes acting on the same aquifer? Two such processes operate at the western boundary, and because they act in opposing directions, neither can be assessed in isolation. Shoreline retreat lowers the ground surface relative to the water table, raising the displacement head and enhancing seaward drainage --- the same mechanism, in reverse sign of intent, as the dune scraping of Section 4.5. Sea-level rise acts oppositely, raising the water table at the coastal boundary. Mapped as companion fields on the same hillshade base as the forest drawdown figure, constructed as set out in Section 3.8.2, these processes are shown in Figure 62 (erosion drawdown from a single shoreline-retreat event), Figure 63 (the sea-level-rise head response as a finite-window transient), and their cell-by-cell difference in Figure 64.

The net map (Figure 64) shows that the two processes do not cancel but partition spatially. A narrow erosion-dominated band lies along the dune-toe margin, coincident with the western Coastal-Forest (C5) and western Western-Residual (C3) wells; this is flanked by a sea-level-rise--dominated rise at the immediate shore and near-neutral conditions across the dune interior. The erosion and sea-level-rise contributions are of comparable magnitude over a matched five-year window, so the western-margin signal is the residual of two opposing processes rather than the action of either alone.

The coastal-drift covariate carried in the clearfell BACI analysis (Section 4.6.3) absorbs this west-to-east deepening gradient; it carries the net field and does not decompose it into its constituent processes (Section 5.5).

These three figures are single-mechanism illustrative constructions on the eroding Caernarfon Bay shore only; they combine a single storm-magnitude retreat event with gradual sea-level rise, and depend on assumed retreat-rate, hydraulic-diffusivity, datum, and window parameters. They illustrate the relative spatial reach of the two processes, not a deterministic forecast or a closed water balance.

### **Episodicity, retreat rates and sea-level counteraction**

The gradient fitted above is a rate averaged over twenty-one years, and the process producing it is not steady. Shoreline retreat at this frontage is episodic: the operative constant in the spatial construction is a single-event retreat of 6 m against the measured 2006--2026 retreat rate E_c = 2.32 m yr⁻¹ (Script 40; Section 3.8.2). Whether the hydraulic boundary has been displaced further than the dune toe over the study window --- the two are not obliged to move together --- is not resolved by this record: the per-driver scale-factor regression returns a coastal scale factor indistinguishable from both zero and unity in every window examined (Section 4.12.1).

Nor is the retreat uniform along the frontage. Pye and Blott (2024) record a north-positive to south-negative gradient, with progradation in the north and chronic retreat concentrated at the southern Twyni Penrhos frontage. A single δ₀ fitted across the network is therefore a frontage average, and the wells nearest the most active section of shoreline are not necessarily those with the smallest d.

Acting against retreat is sea-level rise, which raises the head at the seaward boundary rather than lowering the ground beside it. The two are opposite in sign and differ in inland reach, which is why the fields below partition spatially rather than cancelling: a narrow erosion-dominated band at the dune toe, flanked by a sea-level-rise-dominated rise further inland.

None of this changes the fitted profile. It bounds how it should be read: as a frontage-averaged, time-averaged rate, whose local and episodic realisation the monitoring network is not designed to resolve.

## Management influence on the water table

The spatial reach of forest management perturbations is shown directly by the drawdown propagation analysis (Figure 65), which models the steady-state head perturbation from forest canopy interception as an exponential decay with flow-weighted cost-distance from the forest boundary (λ ≈ 230 m). Estimated drawdown exceeds 50 mm out to about 250 m of flow-weighted cost-distance from the forest edge, decays to 25 mm at CEH23 and 8 mm at CEH6, and is negligible (≤2 mm) at the eastern dune and lake-edge wells CEH24, CEH10 and CEH11. These are steady-state values; the timescale to reach equilibrium is governed by the drainage decay half-life values mapped in Figure 54, ranging from months in the eastern dune (t½ approximately 6--13 months) to years in the forest interior (C4 mean t½ approximately 26 months)* *(Section 5.4.3). Forest management perturbations are therefore concentrated in the forest zone and its margins and decline steeply eastwards across the six eastern wells of the lake-edge cluster, from 73 mm at CEH27 nearest the forest to 8 mm at CEH6 furthest east (CEH26 43 mm, CEH23 25 mm, CEH25 and CEH5 11 mm). The seventh lake-edge well, CEH11, lies 1.7--2.0 km south of that group rather than further east, 1600 m from the forest, and carries 0.4 mm --- the smallest modelled drawdown in the cluster.

The dune scraping of Section 4.5 can be placed on the same spatial footing as the forest and coastal fields. Figure 66 renders the April 2015 CEH36 scrape as a steady-state drain, with edge magnitude anchored to the measured CEH36 response (129 mm) and the same leaky-aquifer decay length as the forest field (λ ≈ 230 m). Modelled drawdown exceeds 50 mm only within \~100 m of the excavation and decays to a few millimetres by the nearest clearfell-tier wells. As with the forest field these are steady-state values: the equilibration time at these distances is years to decades (Section 5.4.3), which is why the uphill propagation is not resolved as a distance-decay signal within the 31-month BACI window (Section 4.5).

## Combined Driver Assessment and Observed Network Change

Figure 67 combines the two non-felling drawdown drivers acting on the clearfell compartment --- the 2015 scrape and a Storm-Brendan-scale retreat event --- as a single head-loss field on the pre-fell baseline. The combined drawdown reaches ≈ 135 mm at the scrape and tapers through the clearfell compartment, with the coastal-erosion term adding a south-western band; the felling step estimated by the BACI ANCOVA (Section 4.6) is the residual once both are accounted for. This is the spatial form of the gradient that the coastal-drift covariate of Section 4.6.3 absorbs: the covariate absorbs the net west-to-east gradient that this figure decomposes into the scrape drain and the coastal retreat.

Four further spatial figures are derived from the framework developed in Sections 4.9.3 and 4.9.4: a measured clearfell step-change map (Figure 68), a parametric net state map superimposing all five active drivers (Figure 69), and an empirical MSL5 change map comparing the pre-clearfell and current MSL5 windows (Figure 71) and a modelled 2005-2025 driver-change map (Figure 70). Methods for all three are in Section 3.8.1; interpretation of the comparison between Figures 68 and 69 is in Section 5.7.5.

Measured clearfell spatial response

The clearfell step-change map (Figure 68) shows the difference in mean water-table level between the pre-felling scraping era and the post-felling era at each well (*fell_step_cc*, Script 10b; positive = shallower after felling). The map shows a broadly positive response across the open dune interior (+25 to +100 mm), with the largest gains at the C4 Forest Control wells immediately adjacent to the felled compartment. A zone of −25 to −100 mm appears along the south-western coastal margin at the C5 Coastal Forest and southern C3 wells. The coastal-margin zone coincides with the coastal-retreat gradient of Section 4.10.2 and with the Coastal Control tier of Section 4.6.4; the positive zone coincides with the C4 and immediately adjacent C3 interior where the BACI step of Section 4.6.3 is measured (Section 5.7.5).

Parametric net state map

Figure 69 (method: Section 3.8.1) superimposes all five annual-mean driver fields on the site grid. The forest interior carries a large net loss (−50 to over −150 mm) where the standing canopy drawdown dominates. A small net-gain zone sits over the felled compartment where the clearfell interception recovery locally exceeds the surrounding forest loss. The open dune is near-neutral: neither the erosion drawdown nor the SLR head gain reaches the eastern dune interior at meaningful magnitude. Along the southern shoreline, a narrow net-gain band reflects SLR marginally exceeding the Storm Brendan erosion drawdown at the immediate dune toe.

![](Pictures/10000001000007FC00000682764275A4.png){width="6.2217in" height="4.3063in"}**Figure : **Net water-table state --- parametric combination of five simultaneous annual-mean drivers: forest canopy drawdown (H₀ = 150 mm, λ ≈ 230 m), clearfell gain (same H₀, λ), dune-scrape contribution (all eight cuts; H₀ measured at CEH36 +130 mm, CEH21 +74 mm, CEH18 +9 mm; others assumed = CEH36; leaky-aquifer superposition with method-of-images coastal correction; scrape footprints contribute +H₀ rise, surrounding area contributes drawdown), coastal erosion (h₀ = 81 mm), SLR (+20 mm over 5 yr). Net = SLR gain + clearfell gain + scrape rise − forest loss − erosion loss − scrape drawdown. Symmetric ±150 mm diverging scale; bold zero contour. First-order superposition of annual-mean fields; not a closed water balance (caveats: Section 4.10.5). (Source: 20_net_state_map.png).

The 2005→2025 driver-change map

The 2005→2025 driver-change map (Figure 70) re-bases the parametric net-state construction to the study record, differencing each modelled driver field between its 2005 and 2025 states so that the map shows what the drivers imply should have changed over the monitoring window rather than the accumulated state since the forest was planted. Because the standing pine canopy is at equilibrium at both endpoints, its drawdown cancels in the difference and the mature forest interior returns to near zero --- the check that the map is an epoch difference and not a re-drawing of Figure 69. Five fields change over the window and are summed: the clearfell gain, computed as in the net-state map from the removal of the interception deficit over the felled compartment; the dune-scrape response, with all cuts within the window contributing; the five-year chronic coastal drawdown; sea-level-rise head gain over the same span; and a broadleaf-restock field new to this map. The broadleaf-restock block, felled in 1993 and restocked in 1995, was already near closed canopy at the 2005 baseline and reaches full canopy by 2025; only the increment of interception deficit that develops over 2005→2025 enters the map, computed on the same exponential-decay construction as the forest field but scaled by the broadleaf interception fraction (0.15, against 0.24 for pine; Komatsu et al., 2011) and by the canopy-establishment increment, giving of order 56 mm of added drawdown at source. It appears as a drawdown patch of the opposite sign to the clearfell gain --- the atmospheric-draw signature of a canopy returning where the clearfell removed one. The coastal-retreat field is expressed as a five-year chronic drawdown, five years of the observed coast-edge decline rate (from the live Script 25 forest-free fit, δ₀ = 31.3 mm yr⁻¹), giving h₀ = 5 × δ₀ ≈ 157 mm at the dune toe on the same five-year horizon as the sea-level-rise field --- the strongest of the five fields at the western coastal margin, and rate-independent by construction. As a first-order superposition of single-mechanism fields the map is illustrative and not a closed water balance; the broadleaf and coastal fields in particular are modelled quantities the dipwell record cannot fully resolve, and are presented as indicative. The map is the modelled companion to the observed climate-removed trend map (Figure 73, Section 3.8) over the same 2005→2025 window: the two are built from different data by different methods and are expected to agree in broad direction rather than in detail, so their agreement where it occurs supports the attribution and their divergence flags a driver the model does not capture.

![**Figure :** Modelled water-table change across Newborough Warren, 2005--2025 --- full-window (20-year) coastal horizon, logarithmic scale. The companion to the five-year driver-change map, showing the same modelled drivers but with the coastal field accumulated over the full study window. The map is the epoch difference of the modelled driver fields (2025 minus 2005): the standing pine canopy is at equilibrium in both epochs and cancels, so the near-white forest interior is the check that the difference is working rather than a re-drawing of the standing-forest drawdown. The drivers that change over the window are the December 2017 clearfell (interception deficit removed → head gain, blue, plotted at the observed BACI step of +113 mm), the broadleaf restock (canopy interception added → head loss, an indicative +56 mm increment as the block approached closed canopy), the 2015 and 2023 dune scrapes (slack rises with surrounding drawdown cones), sea-level rise (+20 mm), and the coastal chronic decline. The coastal field here is the full-window accumulation of the fitted coast-edge trend (20 × δ₀ ≈ 627 mm at the dune toe, decaying to zero at the reach L_cg ≈ 900 m); the five-year companion instead shows the near-term chronic value (≈ 157 mm) for a legible comparison of the management drivers. Because the coastal drawdown (of order several hundred millimetres) is far larger than the management effects (of order one hundred millimetres), the colour scale is logarithmic so both read on one map: deep red marks the strongest coastal drying at the toe, fading through amber to white where change is negligible, and blue marks head gain. The fields are combined by linear superposition; where they overlap the map shows their sum, which is a first-order upper bound and may over-state the true combined drawdown. The map is a modelled prediction surface --- at each well it predicts a 2005--2025 change that can be tested against the observed record (a per-well validation is reported separately); the coastal and broadleaf fields are the least record-constrained and are flagged as modelled. Inland propagation of the coastal signal toward the reach is diffusive and develops over years to decades; the magnitudes shown are the accumulated end-of-window values, not the present-day resolved field. (Source: 20_driver_change_20yr.png)](Pictures/100000010000070D0000058BC19742D0.png "fig:"){width="6.2217in" height="4.972in"}**

[]{#anchor-40}**Observed network change **

Figure 71 presents the conventional two-window reading of observed network change --- validated on its own terms (Section 5.7.5) but, as set out below, limited in what a two-window difference can establish about absolute change.

The MSL5 change map (Figure 71; method: Section 3.8.1) compares window end 2017 (springs 2013--2017, pre-clearfell, network mean −588 mm below ground) with window end 2023 (springs 2019--2023, network mean −685 mm). The raw 2023-minus-2017 difference exceeds the ±25 mm display threshold at 56 of 59 wells, every one of them deepening; no well shallows. Set against the five-year window standard error (78--181 mm by cluster, above), no single well\'s difference is resolved; it is the coherence of sign across the network that carries the signal. The map shows a broadly deeper aquifer in the current window, the deepening intensifying from the eastern dune interior toward the south-western coastal margin. Because the figure differences two five-year windows, every time-invariant driver cancels --- in particular the constant drawdown of the 60-year standing forest, which is present in both windows and contributes nothing to the difference --- so the surviving pattern reflects only drivers that progressed across the study period (Section 5.7.5).

The eastern C1/C2 dune wells deepen least (CEH25 −13, L7 −17, D7 −25 mm), several falling within the ±25 mm near-neutral band. The clearfell Impact well WMC3 (−85 mm) and the scrape well CEH36 (−74 mm) deepen broadly in line with the −97 mm site-wide mean, showing no intervention-specific departure from the surrounding network. The most strongly negative zone is the south-western coastal margin: CEH22 (−229 mm), CEH21 (−194 mm), CEH18 (−158 mm), and the C5 coastal members CEH19, CEH17, NW9 (−150 to −153 mm). These wells lie nearest the eroding coast (Section 4.10.2).

The C4 Forest Control wells deepen by −130 mm (cluster mean), more than the −97 mm site-wide average. These are unfelled controls, and the map applies no climate correction; the excess is read in Section 5.7.5 against the climate-response envelope of Figure 74.

The interannual standard deviation of annual spring level differs widely across the network: about 175 mm at C1, 251 mm at C2, 315 mm at C3, 277 mm at C5 and 404 mm at C4, giving a five-year window mean a standard error of about 78, 112, 141, 124 and 181 mm respectively. Controlling for the drainage recession time, this standard deviation correlates with the atmospheric-draw coefficient β₂ at partial rank r = +0.63 (p \< 0.0001); controlling for β₂, its association with the recession time is not significant (partial r = +0.16, p = 0.20). The two parameters are themselves correlated across wells (Spearman +0.37). Across the 65 wells with at least twelve valid spring years, the lag-1 autocorrelation of annual spring level is approximately zero at every cluster, with cluster means between −0.14 and +0.05, against an expectation of 0.30 at C1 rising to 0.77 at C4 if the fitted drainage term is read as a first-order annual recession; it is uncorrelated with the recession time (Spearman +0.05, p = 0.70), and the site-mean spring series over 21 years gives −0.00.

These results are robust within the two-window method: the spring-gap and independent-metric checks of Section 5.7.5 indicate the 2017→2023 deepening is not an artefact of window length or spring-record gaps. Their limitation is comparative rather than internal. Because the amplitude of interannual variation differs so widely across the network, the absolute magnitude of a two-window difference --- and at some wells its sign --- depends on which two windows are compared, even between windows matched for antecedent rainfall; the matched-window sensitivity analysis of Section 5.7.5 yields site-mean changes spanning −0.14 to +0.22 m and changing sign across all admissible window pairs (19 of 66 falling, 47 rising) --- the −97 mm comparison being one interior point and the wet-2024 windows the +0.22 m extreme --- which is why absolute site-wide change is not rested on this two-window method (Script 34). The −97 mm site-wide figure is therefore specific to the 2017/2023 comparison, not a robust estimate of secular change. The two figures that follow remove this dependence: Figure 72 maps the differential movement with the common climate signal removed, and Figure 74 the climate-response envelope --- the latter quantifying directly the forested clusters' climate response.
