[]{#anchor-41}Secular differential movement

Figure 72 shows the secular differential movement of the spring water table across Newborough Warren: with the common climate signal removed, the forest mound holds its position while the lake-edge and coastal margins decline relative to the site as a whole. The quantity mapped is, for each well, the linear trend through its spring anomaly --- the well's mean-spring level minus the site-mean spring level in the same year --- over 2011--2025. Subtracting the site mean each year removes the shared climate forcing that dominates the raw record, so what remains is the rate at which each well is gaining or losing ground against the rest of the Warren. Because it is built from a per-well trend rather than a two-window difference, the map is insensitive to the window-selection problem of Figure 71; it correlates above 0.98 with the two-window pattern but does not inherit its fragility.

The differential signal is spatially coherent but statistically uneven. Of the 72 wells mapped over 2011--2025, eight reach individual significance under an AR(1)-corrected trend test cross-checked by a moving-block bootstrap; these are predominantly the lake-edge and coastal wells that are losing ground. The forest-interior rise is coherent across neighbouring wells but individually sub-significant --- each forest well is rising slowly against a noisy background --- and it firms up over the longer 2005--2025 window (13 of 75 wells significant). The same holding-up appears in the C5 coastal-forest wells where they sit on the high ground: the inland C4 forest mound holds while C5 wells nearer the eroding coast decline with their open-dune neighbours (Section 5.7.5).

![**Figure :** Secular differential movement of the spring (March,April, May) water table, 2011--2025. For each well the map shows the linear trend (mm yr⁻¹) of its spring anomaly, defined as the well's mean-spring level minus the site-mean spring level in the same year, so that the common climate signal is removed and only movement relative to the site remains. Read as a management diagnostic, it shows the direction and rate at which the spring water table is moving across the site over the study period - which areas are holding or gaining ground relative to the Warren as a whole, and which are losing it --- the differential complement to the site-wide drying trend. Solid markers are significant under an AR(1)-corrected trend test corroborated by a moving-block bootstrap; hollow markers are not individually significant. Warm colours rise relative to the site, cool colours decline. CEH13 and CEH14 (SSM outliers) and the Llyn Rhos-Ddu lake gauge are excluded. (Source: 32_differential_movement_2011_2025.png)](Pictures/100000010000064D000004D3E5D5C57C.png "fig:"){width="6.2217in" height="4.7055in"}

*****Absolute movement with the climate signal removed *****

Figure 72 measures each well against the network mean, and over a wet-spring-lifted window that referencing can invert the plain reading: a well that is holding steady while the site mean rises appears to decline, and a slow-draining well reads as rising while falling more slowly than the rest. Figure 73 removes that ambiguity by mapping the absolute secular trend at each well --- the shared climate signal taken out by regression against an external climatic-water-balance index, but with no re-referencing to the network mean, so brown marks ground where the water table is genuinely falling and blue where it is genuinely holding or rising. The construction and window are described in Section 3.8.1; the trend is fitted over 2005--2025, the longer window being primary here because the shorter window is dominated by wells whose records begin only after 2011.

The absolute map is more spatially specific than the differential one. Once the weather is removed, most of the Warren is close to holding its position --- the lake-edge, dune and main-forest clusters all sit within a few millimetres per year of zero (C1 +2.1, C2 +4.6, C4 +2.7 mm yr⁻¹) --- and the weather-independent losses are confined to the western and coastal margins. The coastal-forest cluster carries much the most negative trend (C5 ≈ −11.6 mm yr⁻¹), and the western residual cluster is mildly negative (C3 ≈ −3.4 mm yr⁻¹); the strongest individual driers are the western and coastal wells (CEH3 −28, NW9 −23, CEH4 −19 mm yr⁻¹). This is the coastal-margin decline that Figure 72 identifies as the fastest-losing part of the network, in absolute terms: the forest interior is stable rather than recovering. Figure 72 answers which part of the Warren is gaining or losing ground against the rest and Figure 73 where the water table is rising or falling; the two agree on the coastal margin (Section 5.7.5).

![](Pictures/1000000100000633000004D393698DED.png){width="6.2217in" height="4.8791in"}**Figure :** Absolute climate-removed secular trend of the spring (March, April, May) water table, 2005--2025. For each well the spring level is regressed jointly on an external spring climatic-water-balance index (RAF Valley) and a linear time term, and the fitted time coefficient is the secular trend in mm yr⁻¹, with the climate signal removed but without re-referencing to the network mean. Blue = genuinely rising or holding; brown = genuinely falling. Solid markers reach individual significance (AR(1)-corrected, bootstrap cross-checked); hollow do not. Wells lacking a genuine pre-window record are excluded (Section 3.8.1). The coastal and western margins carry the genuine secular losses; the interior, including the forest, holds once the weather is removed. (Source: 36_absolute_climate_trend_2005_2025.png.)

[]{#anchor-42}The climate-response envelope

Where Figure 72 measures slow secular change, Figure 74 measures climate sensitivity: how far each part of the network moves between the driest and wettest springs the record contains, and Figure 75 how close the dry-year water table already lies to ecological thresholds. The amplification panel (Figure 74) addresses the first. Between its antecedent-dry and antecedent-wet spring extremes the site-mean water table swings approximately 0.75 m; expressing each well's swing as a ratio to that network-mean swing, with the common-mode removed, gives a relative amplification field independent of window choice, because it compares true end-members rather than adjacent windows. The forest interior amplifies the shared swing to about 1.7×, while the lake edge damps it to about 0.6×, with the open dune close to unity. This is the behaviour behind the C4 deepening of Figure 71 (Section 5.7.5). The amplification correlates most strongly with the atmospheric-draw coefficient β₂ (r ≈ +0.8), which survives control for elevation and exclusion of the forest clusters.

The second panel (Figure 75) maps the dry-year spring water-table depth --- the mean spring level across the dry extreme years (2011, 2012, 2019). Spring is used in preference to the summer minimum because the spring record is near-complete whereas summer-minimum readings are sparse; the choice is deliberately conservative, since spring is the seasonal high and therefore the shallowest the water table reaches in those years. On this panel the Curreli et al. (2013) thresholds are overlaid not as summer-minimum crossings but to mark where even this spring high has already fallen below wet-slack (SD15b, 0.61 m) and dry-slack (SD16, 0.98 m) viability. Because the summer minimum lies deeper still, the contoured zones are a strict lower bound on the area below ecological viability: where the forest interior and western dune sit beyond SD16 even in spring, the water table is below dry-slack viability for the whole of those dry years. Together the two panels separate the two questions that the single two-window map of Figure 71 conflated --- how sensitive each area is to climate, and how close it already sits to ecological thresholds in dry years --- neither of which depends on an arbitrary choice of comparison window.

![](Pictures/1000000100000626000004EF869435E5.png){width="6.2217in" height="4.6902in"}**Figure : **The climate-response envelope of the spring water table. Relative amplification field --- each well's dry-to-wet spring swing as a ratio to the network-mean swing (≈0.73 m), with the common-mode removed; values above one amplify the shared climate swing, below one damp it. Wells with full dry-extreme coverage build the interpolated surface; a well below the confidence threshold would be drawn off-surface as an open triangle, and none is in this partition. The Llyn Rhos-Ddu gauge excluded. (Source: 33_amplification_field.png).

![](Pictures/1000000100000636000004EF4D9ECC2C.png){width="6.2217in" height="4.1937in"}

**Figure :** The climate-response envelope of the spring water table: Dry-year spring water-table depth --- mean spring level across the dry extreme years (2011, 2012, 2019), with the Curreli et al. (2013) SD15b (0.61 m, wet slack) and SD16 (0.98 m, dry slack) thresholds contoured. []{#anchor-43}Summary of pattern

Figure 69 predicts a large net loss across the forest interior under the parametric annual-mean drivers, and the 2017/2023 window comparison (Figure 71) shows a broadly deeper aquifer with the largest declines at the south-western coastal margin; but the absolute site-wide deepening is specific to that window pair (Section 5.7.5). Figure 72 shows, with the common climate signal removed, the coastal-margin decline as the largest secular movement and the forest interior holding its position relative to the rest of the Warren. The per-cluster rates quantify this split: C4 Main Forest rises at a cluster mean of +13.7 mm yr*⁻¹* relative to the site (range +6.9 to +18.9 mm yr*⁻¹* across the seven mapped C4 wells; none individually significant after AR(1) correction); C1 Lake Edge declines at −5.6 mm yr*⁻¹* (CEH11 significant, p = 0.048); C5 Coastal Forest at −8.5 mm yr*⁻¹* (NW9, CEH17 and CEH19 significant, p = 0.016, 0.046 and 0.020); and C2 Dune is approximately neutral (+0.3 mm yr*⁻¹*). CEH22, at the south-western coastal margin, is the most rapidly declining well in the network at −27.8 mm yr*⁻¹* (p \< 0.001). The site-mean spring trend over 2011--2025 is +19.8 mm yr*⁻¹* (AR-corrected p = 0.284; bootstrap CI −3.4 to +43.2 mm yr*⁻¹*), with the exceptionally wet springs of 2021 and 2024 in the window; Figure 72 shows the forest rising relative to the network, not in absolute terms.

Figure 74 shows the forest amplifying the dry-to-wet climate swing more strongly than any other zone (C4 mean 1.66×, range 1.31--2.32×; C1 lake edge 0.64×; open dune near unity). The amplification correlates positively with β₂ (r ≈ +0.74) and negatively with β₃ (r = −0.49, p \< 0.001) (Section 5.7.5).

The felled well FE2 (inside the December 2017 clearfell boundary) registers a spring differential trend of +8.8 mm yr*⁻¹* (Figure 72) and a co-temporal amplification of 1.21× (Figure 74). Both values lie notably below the unfelled C4 interior mean (+13.7 mm yr*⁻¹*; 1.66×). FE2\'s wet-year spring depth (−1.00 m) rises less than the surrounding unfelled C4 reference wells (mean wet-year depth −0.54 m), and its swing (763 mm) is substantially smaller than the C4 mean (1,135 mm). The summer drought floor at FE2 (−1.77 m in dry years) is slightly deeper than the C4 reference mean (−1.67 m). FE1, approximately 20 m outside the felled boundary, matches the unfelled interior on the differential trend (+15.3 mm yr*⁻¹*) and sits just below it on amplification (1.54×). Their reading against the clearfell result of Section 4.6 is in Section 5.5.1.

The reconciliation of the parametric prediction with the observed change --- the window-sensitivity of the absolute deepening, the differential movement of Figure 72, and the climate amplification of Figure 74 --- is taken up in Section 5.7.5.

### Driver validation and comparative footing

The differential pattern above identifies where the network is moving, but not how much of that movement each modelled driver accounts for. Two diagnostics address this, and their shared conclusion is cautious: the network can bound the drivers\' relative footing, but cannot independently confirm the coastal-retreat amplitude from the monitoring record alone.

A per-driver scale-factor regression (Section 3.8.1) fits the climate-corrected per-well change against the modelled coastal and clearfell fields as separate regressors, together with a free spatially-uniform intercept that absorbs the site-wide background decline present even at unfelled control wells. The scale factors are not uniformly indeterminate. In the window where each driver acts, its factor is distinguishable from zero but not from unity: the coastal factor is 3.06 (95% CI 0.27 to 5.85) over the pre-intervention 2006--2012 window, and the clearfell factor 2.21 (0.67 to 3.74) over the post-clearfell 2018--2025 window; over the full 2005--2025 record the coastal factor is 0.48 (−0.03 to 1.00), spanning zero narrowly, and the clearfell factor, −0.47 (−3.25 to 2.31), is unresolved. The uniform intercept is consistently well-determined and large --- a decline of 520 mm over 2006--2012 (95% CI −589 to −451) and a rise of 269 mm over 2018--2025 (222 to 315) --- so the dominant secular movement in the network remains common-mode rather than spatially structured by any single modelled driver. The regression explains a modest fraction of the between-well variance (R² 0.10 and 0.11 in the two shorter windows, 0.35 over the full record, and 0.25 in the broadleaf-covariate variant). In that variant the broadleaf-restock covariate is −3.47 (−6.17 to −0.77), and the clearfell factor, 1.79 (0.83 to 2.75), keeps its footing when the covariate is carried. The full-record window is fitted on 20 wells against 40 in the two shorter windows, because it requires a well to carry a trend across the whole span.

This is a bounded confirmation rather than a measurement of amplitude. Each driver field is detectable in the window where it acts, at a scale consistent with the modelled amplitude, but the intervals are wide --- a factor of three in the coastal case --- and the reasons are the ones that limit the test: the coastal signature is collinear with easting (r ≈ −0.48) and with the underlying clay-dip substrate gradient, the per-well residual scatter (of order ±150--200 mm) is of the same size as the driver amplitudes being tested, and only around fifteen of the wells entering the fit carry a modelled coastal amplitude large enough to constrain the regression at all. The coastal shape (δ₀, L_cg) is moreover fitted from this same network via the gradient analysis of Section 4.10.2, so the scale-factor test is in part self-confirming; the one genuinely independent check is an expanding-window trajectory of the implied coastal decline rate, which is itself too contaminated by the 2006--2012 drought signal to be conclusive. The regression detects the coastal field without resolving its amplitude; the background common-mode movement is the larger term in every window.

A complementary analysis (Section 3.8.1) places the drivers on a common footing over the 2005--2025 horizon, using observed BACI anchors where available (clearfell +112.8 mm; on-site scraping +129.4 mm; the reproducible WMC3 off-site scrape drawdown of −55 mm) and modelled fields elsewhere. The unexplained uniform decline of Section 4.10.2 is carried on the same footing at −11.0 mm yr⁻¹, as a central estimate the record does not resolve. The panel\'s fitted constant is not used for it: that quantity is not separately identified from the cumulative-water-balance covariate, and only their sum is recovered. Expressed as a local water-table depth change, the coastal driver is the largest of the spatially-structured terms: a lowering of up to approximately 157 mm at the dune toe, tapering inland over a reach of roughly 900 m; its depth-against-distance profile, alongside those of the forest and scraping drivers, is shown in Figure 81 --- which draws only terms that vary with distance. On the area-integrated volume and the ecological-threshold measures (Figure 77) the ordering inverts: the unexplained uniform decline is the largest single term, because it acts across the whole site rather than a fringe, while the coastal drawdown --- deeper than anything else but confined to the western dune field --- is second. The inversion rests on a central estimate for the uniform term and not on a resolved rate, and is stated on that footing. Dune scraping produces a net site-wide loss because its off-site drainage cone draws down the water table across the area surrounding each cut by more than the on-site slack rise recovers; integrated across the site, the net scraping effect is of order 26% of the coastal drawdown in magnitude (Section 5.4.3). Sea-level rise, evaluated on the near-term five-year projection rather than the twenty-year horizon of the other terms, is indicative only and small by comparison. Both diagnostics are first-order and do not close a water budget; the modelled coastal drawdown remains a projection anchored on the observed δ₀ and unconfirmed spatially by the network, while the off-site scrape drawdown is measured --- reproducibly --- at WMC3. The ranking on the two footings is taken up in Section 5.8.2. The expanding-window trajectory of the implied coastal decline rate --- the one genuinely independent test of the coastal signal --- is shown in Figure 76, and the comparative footing of all drivers in Figure 77.

![**Figure : **Independent test of the chronic coastal-drying assumption: implied coastal decline rate δ₀ from the coast-only scale-factor regression re-run on expanding windows (2005--2010 through 2005--2025). For each window the implied δ₀ is the fitted coastal scale factor multiplied by the assumed rate (the Section 4.10.2 headline δ₀, dashed line). A trajectory that stays above zero throughout is the signature a steadily propagating erosional drawdown would produce --- the coast-to-inland gradient steepening year on year; the value relative to the 29 mm yr⁻¹ line then indicates whether that drawdown is proceeding at, above, or below the assumed chronic rate. A dip to zero indicates no detectable coastal signal on this line (a flat head difference, consistent with static substrate geometry rather than a moving erosional boundary), and a value below zero would indicate a reversing gradient that refutes chronic coastal drawdown --- though in the short early windows a near-zero value more likely reflects insufficient statistical power to resolve the signal than a genuine absence of it. The three fully pre-clearfell windows (ending 2010, 2013, 2016) are the only clean coast-only reads but are individually too noisy --- the earliest is dominated by the 2006--2012 drought --- to establish a stable rate; the windows ending 2019 or later, ringed in orange, span the December 2017 clearfell without a term to absorb its recovery signal, so their implied δ₀ is an upper bound on the coastal contribution rather than a direct estimate. The test is therefore inconclusive on the amplitude: it neither confirms nor refutes the modelled coastal rate, whereas the windowed scale-factor regression in the text separates the coastal field from zero in the pre-intervention window without resolving its size. (Source: 37_implied_delta0_trajectory.png)](Pictures/10000001000007D8000004F745899D65.png "fig:"){width="4.8528in" height="3.0717in"}

## []{#anchor-44}**Scenario Analysis**

The per-well SSM coefficients derived in Section 4.9 were used to project equilibrium water table responses under prescribed climate and forest management perturbations, following the framework of Section 3.8. Six scenarios were evaluated: baseline; UKCP18 2050s and 2080s climate trajectories; full clearfell; 50% thinning; and broadleaf conversion. Scenario difference maps were computed as Δh = h(scenario) − h(baseline) for each well, season and cluster. The full per-scenario, per-season, per-cluster Δh output is available through the Newborough Warren Hydrogeological Modelling Suite (Hollingham, 2026), an interactive web-based scenario viewer that renders the per-well Δh field across the site using IDW interpolation, with a complementary depth-below-surface view masked to hydrologically meaningful slack positions and overlaid with the Curreli et al. (2013) SD15b/SD16 ecological thresholds. The cluster-level results are summarized below.

### []{#anchor-45}Climate Scenario Projections

Climate scenario responses follow the per-cluster β coefficient structure. Under UKCP18 2050s forcing, the site-wide mean annual Δh is −0.018 m/month, with cluster-level annual responses ranging from −0.026 m/month at C4 (Main Forest) to −0.009 m/month at C1 (Lake Edge). Under UKCP18 2080s forcing, the site-wide mean annual response deepens to −0.033 m/month, with a maximum of −0.047 m/month at C4 and a minimum of −0.017 m/month at C1. Both UKCP18 scenarios show the forested clusters carrying the largest annual declines, where β₂ is highest and net recharge is reduced by interception. The annual response conceals a pronounced seasonal asymmetry. Under both trajectories, winter Δh is positive at all clusters (site-wide mean +0.028 m/month at 2050s and +0.056 m/month at 2080s) as the increased winter rainfall under RCP8.5 Wales outpaces the concurrent increase in winter PET. Summer Δh is strongly negative and carries the annual signal: site-wide means of −0.064 m/month at 2050s and −0.121 m/month at 2080s, reaching −0.134 m/month at C2 under the 2080s trajectory. The summer-dominated signature is discussed with the observed record in Section 5.7.1.

The same projection framework, applied to the five-year mean spring water level (MSL5; Section 4.8.3), gives a markedly smaller response than the summer-minimum metric. The projected MSL5 shift is −12 to −21 mm across the clusters at the 2050s horizon and −21 to −39 mm at the 2080s horizon (Figure 78), against summer Δh of −38 to −70 mm and −71 to −134 mm respectively over the same horizons. The MSL5 response is three to five times smaller than the summer response in every cluster and at both horizons. MSL5 is computed over the March--May spring window, which receives the projected increase in winter--spring rainfall; the summer minimum receives the projected increase in summer atmospheric demand and the projected reduction in summer rainfall (Section 5.7.1). No reference value is defined for a spring mean (Section 4.8.3), so the projected MSL5 shifts are read against the metric\'s own structure rather than against the Curreli et al. (2013) values: at 21--39 mm by the 2080s they are an order of magnitude smaller than the spacing between clusters on MSL5 and than the well-to-well spread within them, and they change no cluster\'s position relative to another. The parallel summer-minimum deterioration is read against the reference values directly (Section 4.8.1), where the open-dune clusters\' summer minima already sit below the SD15b community mean. The implication for the binding ecological constraint is taken up in Section 5.2.5.

![**Figure :** Projected shift in the five-year mean spring water level (ΔMSL5, blue) compared with the projected shift in summer-minimum water level (Δsummer-minimum, orange), by cluster, under UKCP18 RCP8.5 forcing: 2050s (upper panel) and 2080s (lower panel). All shifts are negative (deeper, drier); bar length is the magnitude of the projected deepening in millimetres. In every cluster and at both horizons the summer-minimum response is three to five times the MSL5 response --- the spring baseline metric is comparatively insulated against the projected trajectory while the summer minimum is highly exposed (Section 4.13.1). The contrast is seasonal in origin: the March--May window over which MSL5 is computed receives the projected increase in winter--spring rainfall, partly offsetting the rise in spring evaporative demand, whereas the summer minimum receives the full projected increase in summer atmospheric demand compounded by the projected reduction in summer rainfall. ΔMSL5 values are the cluster-centroid projections from Script 26b; Δsummer-minimum values are the seasonal-mean Δh from the Script 19 scenario framework (Section 4.13.1). ### []{#anchor-46}Forest Management Scenarios

Forest management scenarios produce responses at the two forested clusters (C4 and C5), with a negligible response elsewhere --- exactly zero at C1 and C2, and under 6 mm/month at C3, where two wells sit beneath the pine canopy and so receive the interception change. Full clearfell is modelled by setting canopy interception to 0% and adjusting β₂ at C4 and C5 wells. Fifty percent thinning halves interception from 24% to 12% with proportional β₂ adjustment. Broadleaf conversion replaces the Corsican pine canopy interception fraction of 24% (Freeman, 2008) with an annual-mean deciduous interception of 15% (Komatsu et al., 2011), and applies a seasonally varying β₂ adjustment to reflect deciduous phenology: β₂ follows the winter and summer broadleaf coefficients derived in Section 3.8, held near baseline during the leafless dormant season (November--March) and raised during the growing season to reflect the comparable transpiration rates of mature deciduous and Corsican pine canopy in full leaf.

Under full clearfell with the BACI-corrected β₂ multiplier (Section 3.8), the framework predicts a modest annual water table rise at both forest clusters (C4: +0.041 m/month head, equivalent to +10.5 mm w.e./month volumetric; C5: +0.042 m/month head, +12.8 mm w.e./month). The annual response is driven primarily by the winter recharge gain from canopy removal (C4: +0.050 m/month head; C5: +0.050 m/month head). The summer response is positive but smaller at both clusters (C4: +0.036 m/month, +9.0 mm w.e./month; C5: +0.037 m/month, +11.3 mm w.e./month), reflecting that the winter interception gain exceeds the summer β₂ cost across the year at both substrates. Fifty percent thinning produces a similar pattern at reduced magnitude (C4: +0.021 m/month annually, +5.2 mm w.e./month; C5: +0.021 m/month, +6.4 mm w.e./month). These are steady-state predictions from the SSM coefficient structure; the predicted direction is consistent with the BACI monitoring record, which detects a significant mean monthly recovery at the Impact tier (+113 mm against the Forest control; Section 4.6.3) but no corresponding improvement in summer minima (Section 4.6.4; further interpreted in Section 5.5).

Broadleaf conversion produces a near-neutral annual response at both forest clusters (C4: +0.012 m/month head; C5: +0.014 m/month head), masking a pronounced seasonal asymmetry: winter head-space values are among the largest of any forestry scenario (C4: +0.025 m/month; C5: +0.022 m/month) reflecting the near-zero interception under leafless canopy during the recharge season, but the summer response is negative at C4 (−0.012 m/month, −2.9 mm w.e./month) and near-zero at C5 (+0.001 m/month, +0.4 mm w.e./month) as the growing-season transpiration penalty under mature deciduous canopy consumes the interception gain. The net annual volumetric effect is +2.9 mm w.e./month at C4 and +4.2 mm w.e./month at C5 --- positive at both, but well under a third of the clearfell gain, and at C4 a winter gain (+6.3 mm w.e./month) against a summer cost. The seasonal partition is interpreted in Section 5.5.2.

Site-wide means under forest management are small (annual +0.009 m/month clearfell, +0.004 m/month thinning) because only 14 of 66 reference wells are in the two forest clusters and the framework applies no spatial propagation from the forest zone into other clusters. Broadleaf conversion produces no meaningful site-wide signal.

## Out-of-sample tests against earlier records

Every result in this study is fitted to the 2005--2026 record and tested inside it. Two earlier observations of this aquifer exist: a dipwell record held by Natural Resources Wales for 1989--96 at nine wells of the present network, and Ranwell\'s 1951--53 readings. Both are run as hindcasts from the modern per-well coefficients with no refitting (Scripts 39 and 44); what each can and cannot establish is set out in Sections 5.7.8 and 5.7.9.

### The 1989--96 record

The Natural Resources Wales record covers nine wells of the present network between May 1989 and April 1996, eighty-two monthly observations per well, ending nine years before the modern record opens. Data provenance and permission: the records were supplied for this study; access is covered by the Environmental Information Regulations 2004, and re-use and republication are governed by the Open Government Licence v3.0, under which Natural Resources Wales has confirmed these records may be reproduced with the attribution "Contains Natural Resources Wales information © Natural Resources Wales and database right. All rights reserved." The derived results below are this study\'s own; the underlying records are not.

The test uses each well\'s own coefficients from the modern per-well fit, driven by the RAF Valley climate record for 1989--96, with no refitting and no parameter free to absorb the difference between the epochs. Historic depths are reduced to the present ground surface through each well\'s measured upstand, so the two epochs sit on one datum. Simulation begins from an equilibrium head and the initial condition is immaterial: the spin-up is long enough that varying the starting level across the probed range changes no well\'s result at four decimal places. Of the thirteen historic well codes, twelve are matched to present wells and one remains unidentified and is excluded; at one well, fifteen of eighty-two months sit at the pipe base and are treated as left-censored.

The reduction can be checked against a published figure that the analysis did not use. The annual range of water-table elevation at Newborough over 1989--95 has been reported independently as 0.75 m, with a standard deviation of 0.27 m (Davy et al., 2010); the series reduced here returns 0.725 m with a standard deviation of 0.255 m across fifty-one well-years, an agreement to 0.025 m on a quantity neither study derived from the other.

Across the nine wells the correlation between observed and predicted monthly levels has a median of 0.859 and runs from 0.660 to 0.945. Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency is negative at five of the nine wells while the bias-removed efficiency reaches 0.35 to 0.87. The mean residual --- observed level less predicted --- is −0.057 m across the nine wells and +0.069 m across the six cleanest, so the climate-only prediction sits within about 0.07 m of the observations in both directions.

The epoch shift compares each well\'s mean over 1989--96 with its mean over the modern record. All nine are negative, from −0.132 m to −0.835 m with a median of −0.582 m: the water table of the early 1990s stood lower than it stands today at every well. Six of the nine wells were open ground in 1989 and are open ground now, and they carry the cleanest signal: a median correlation of 0.910, a median bias-removed efficiency of 0.818, and a median epoch shift of −0.338 m. The remaining three have all changed canopy state or sat under canopy throughout, and both their fits and their shifts are worse; the well that has been forest across both epochs is simultaneously the poorest fit in the set and the largest shift.

The comparison window is the driest sustained stretch in the ninety-five-year RAF Valley record: rainfall averages 0.770 m yr⁻¹ over 1989--96 against 0.886 m yr⁻¹ over the modern record, and the surplus of rainfall over potential evapotranspiration is +0.127 m yr⁻¹ against +0.237 m yr⁻¹. What is left over at the six open-ground wells is +0.069 m against a contrast of −0.338 m. The reading of the epoch shift, and what it does not resolve, is in Section 5.7.8.

### The 1951--53 record

The only observation of this aquifer older than the 1989--96 record is Ranwell\'s. Between February 1951 and August 1953 he read seventeen galvanised pipes across the open slacks of the Warren at least fortnightly, levelled each to Ordnance Datum in 1951 and re-surveyed the mobile-dune sites in 1953, and published the result as a seasonal range of 70--100 cm and a set of figures (Ranwell, 1959). He printed no table. Three of the series survive as plotted points (his Sites 1, 4 and 8) and seven more as monthly ranges, and these were recovered from the published figures to about a centimetre; the two figures are independent digitisations of the same readings and agree at the sites they share. The pipes stood in the Penlon and Clwt Gwlyb slacks and in the coastal slack south of them; none stood under the plantation, which was then being planted, and none stood in the slack of his Sites 2--15 for which he printed no series. Where the pipes stood is known to the slack and, on sloping ground, to a few metres: his site sketch is not metric, but his levelled heights agree with the modern terrain model to within the scatter of the placement (median offset 0.16 m, spread 0.14 m), and every site falls in the terrain basin the sketch draws it in.

Two tests follow. The first is the 1989--96 test taken thirty-eight years further back. Each of Ranwell\'s plotted sites is paired with the modern wells that share its terrain basin and lie within 300 m of it, and each paired well\'s own coefficients from the modern fit are driven by the RAF Valley record from 1930, with no refitting. Because the pipe and the well are not at the same point, the comparison is made after removing the mean level difference between them, and because a flooded slack reads at the ground, the modelled level is capped at the surface. What remains is a test of the dynamics alone (Script 44; Figure 79): at the nearest paired well the correlation between Ranwell\'s monthly means and the hindcast is 0.74, 0.75 and 0.91 at the three sites, the seasonal range is reproduced to within a tenth of a metre at each, and the month of the 1951 minimum is the same in the observations and the model at all three. Across every same-basin pairing the correlation runs from 0.70 to 0.91 and the bias-removed efficiency from 0.32 to 0.80, the lower values belonging to the Penlon site, where the modelled 1951--52 winter rise overshoots readings that the pipe could not follow above the ground. The forcing can be checked over exactly these years, because Ranwell also published the rainfall at the Parc Mawr nursery: over his reading span it totals 0.97 of the RAF Valley figure, with a monthly correlation of 0.92.

Points are the monthly means of his fortnightly readings at Sites 1 (Penlon slack), 4 (Clwt Gwlyb) and 8 (the coastal slack); the line is the modern per-well model at the nearest dipwell in the same terrain basin (ceh25, ceh27, nw5), driven by RAF Valley climate from 1930 with the coefficients fitted to 2005--2026, shifted by the mean level difference between pipe and well and capped at the ground surface (dotted), which is where a flooded slack reads. Correlations and bias-removed efficiencies are given in the text (Script 44). (Source: 44_07b_hindcast_report.png)](Pictures/100000010000074E00000620E62A0442.png "fig:"){width="6.2201in" height="5.2165in"}

The second test asks whether the level has moved. Ranwell\'s mean level at each of the eight printed sites, in metres above Ordnance Datum through his own levelling, is set against the modern mean water-table surface interpolated to that point from the wells around it, less the difference the climate of the two periods would produce on its own --- the hindcast\'s own 1951--53 mean against its modern mean at the paired well, which is within 0.05 m of zero at every site. The comparison is not point to point, and its error budget says so: the leave-one-out error of the interpolated surface, the surface gradient times the positional uncertainty of the pipe, the difference between a reading mean and a mid-range mean, and the spread of Ranwell\'s datum against the terrain model, combined in quadrature, give per-site uncertainties of 0.23 to 0.37 m in the Penlon and Clwt Gwlyb slacks and about 0.7 m at the two coastal-slack sites, where the modern surface rests on a single well. Six of the eight sites stand within 0.3 m of their 1951--53 level; the two Clwt Gwlyb sites furthest from a modern well stand about 0.3 and 0.4 m lower, at 1.3 and 1.9 standard errors; and Site 8, at the seaward end of the coastal slack that Ranwell himself recorded as accreting, stands 1.3 m lower against one well 118 m away and is reported rather than explained. No site differs at two standard errors. Weighted by their uncertainties the eight sites give a change of −0.09 ± 0.10 m over the sixty-six years between the midpoints of the two records, with a scatter about that mean of 1.4 times what the error budget predicts; the six sites whose modern surface is well constrained give −0.07 ± 0.11 m. The reading of this bound is in Section 5.7.9.
